Consider a circle of radius \(R=1\). An \(n\)-sided regular polygon consists of \(n\) congruent isosceles triangles with central angle \(\frac{2\pi}{n}\).
1. Area of the inscribed regular \(n\)-gon (\(I_{n}\)):
Each of the \(n\) triangles has two sides of length \(R=1\) and included angle \(\frac{2\pi}{n}\):
\[I_{n}=n \cdot \left( \frac{1}{2} \cdot 1^{2} \cdot \sin \frac{2\pi}{n} \right)=\frac{n}{2}\sin \frac{2\pi}{n} \Longrightarrow \sin \frac{2\pi}{n}=\frac{2I_{n}}{n}\quad \text{--- (1)}\]
2. Area of the circumscribed regular \(n\)-gon (\(O_{n}\)):
Each of the \(n\) triangles has altitude (inradius) \(R=1\) and base \(2\tan \frac{\pi}{n}\):
\[O_{n}=n \cdot \left( \frac{1}{2} \cdot 1 \cdot 2\tan \frac{\pi}{n} \right)=n\tan \frac{\pi}{n}\quad \text{--- (2)}\]
Now express \(\frac{I_{n}}{O_{n}}\) using (1) and (2):
\[\frac{I_{n}}{O_{n}}=\frac{\frac{n}{2}\sin \frac{2\pi}{n}}{n\tan \frac{\pi}{n}}=\frac{\frac{n}{2}\left( 2\sin \frac{\pi}{n}\cos \frac{\pi}{n} \right)}{n\frac{\sin(\pi/n)}{\cos(\pi/n)}}=\cos^{2}\frac{\pi}{n}=\frac{1 + \cos \frac{2\pi}{n}}{2}\]
Using \(\cos \frac{2\pi}{n}=\sqrt{1 - \sin^{2}\frac{2\pi}{n}}\) and substituting \(\sin \frac{2\pi}{n}=\frac{2I_{n}}{n}\) from (1):
\[\frac{I_{n}}{O_{n}}=\frac{1}{2}\left( 1 + \sqrt{1 - \sin^{2}\frac{2\pi}{n}} \right)=\frac{1}{2}\left( 1 + \sqrt{1 - \left( \frac{2I_{n}}{n} \right)^{2}} \right)\]
\[\Longrightarrow I_{n}=\frac{O_{n}}{2}\left( 1 + \sqrt{1 - \left( \frac{2I_{n}}{n} \right)^{2}} \right)\quad \text{(Hence Proved)}\]

IIT200300000Q19:
Since \(\overrightarrow{u},\overrightarrow{v},\overrightarrow{w}\) are unit vectors and the angle between \(\overrightarrow{u}\) and \(\overrightarrow{v}\) is \(\alpha\), the magnitude of \(\overrightarrow{u} + \overrightarrow{v}\) is:
\[\left| \overrightarrow{u} + \overrightarrow{v} \right|=\sqrt{\left| \overrightarrow{u} \right|^{2} + \left| \overrightarrow{v} \right|^{2} + 2\overrightarrow{u} \cdot \overrightarrow{v}}=\sqrt{1 + 1 + 2\cos \alpha}=\sqrt{4\cos^{2}\frac{\alpha}{2}}=2\cos \frac{\alpha}{2}\]
Therefore, the unit vectors \(\overrightarrow{x},\overrightarrow{y},\overrightarrow{z}\) along the internal angle bisectors are:
\[\overrightarrow{x}=\frac{\overrightarrow{u} + \overrightarrow{v}}{2\cos \frac{\alpha}{2}},\quad \overrightarrow{y}=\frac{\overrightarrow{v} + \overrightarrow{w}}{2\cos \frac{\beta}{2}},\quad \overrightarrow{z}=\frac{\overrightarrow{w} + \overrightarrow{u}}{2\cos \frac{\gamma}{2}}\]
Recall two standard identities of scalar triple products:
1. \(\left[ \overrightarrow{x} \times \overrightarrow{y}\quad \overrightarrow{y} \times \overrightarrow{z}\quad \overrightarrow{z} \times \overrightarrow{x} \right]=\left[ \overrightarrow{x}\quad \overrightarrow{y}\quad \overrightarrow{z} \right]^{2}\)
2. \(\left[ \overrightarrow{u} + \overrightarrow{v}\quad \overrightarrow{v} + \overrightarrow{w}\quad \overrightarrow{w} + \overrightarrow{u} \right]=2\left[ \overrightarrow{u}\quad \overrightarrow{v}\quad \overrightarrow{w} \right]\)
First compute \(\left[ \overrightarrow{x}\quad \overrightarrow{y}\quad \overrightarrow{z} \right]\):
\[\left[ \overrightarrow{x}\quad \overrightarrow{y}\quad \overrightarrow{z} \right]=\frac{\left[ \overrightarrow{u} + \overrightarrow{v}\quad \overrightarrow{v} + \overrightarrow{w}\quad \overrightarrow{w} + \overrightarrow{u} \right]}{8\cos \frac{\alpha}{2}\cos \frac{\beta}{2}\cos \frac{\gamma}{2}}=\frac{2\left[ \overrightarrow{u}\quad \overrightarrow{v}\quad \overrightarrow{w} \right]}{8\cos \frac{\alpha}{2}\cos \frac{\beta}{2}\cos \frac{\gamma}{2}}=\frac{1}{4}\left[ \overrightarrow{u}\quad \overrightarrow{v}\quad \overrightarrow{w} \right]\sec \frac{\alpha}{2}\sec \frac{\beta}{2}\sec \frac{\gamma}{2}\]
Squaring both sides yields:
\[\left[ \overrightarrow{x} \times \overrightarrow{y}\quad \overrightarrow{y} \times \overrightarrow{z}\quad \overrightarrow{z} \times \overrightarrow{x} \right]=\left[ \overrightarrow{x}\quad \overrightarrow{y}\quad \overrightarrow{z} \right]^{2}=\frac{1}{16}\left[ \overrightarrow{u}\quad \overrightarrow{v}\quad \overrightarrow{w} \right]^{2}\sec^{2}\frac{\alpha}{2}\sec^{2}\frac{\beta}{2}\sec^{2}\frac{\gamma}{2}\quad \text{(Hence Proved)}\]

Let \(r(t)\) and \(h(t)\) denote the radius of the top circular liquid surface and the depth of the liquid in the cone at time \(t\), respectively. Initially at \(t=0\), the cone is full, so \(h(0)=H\) and \(r(0)=R\).
By similar triangles in the vertical cross-section of the cone:
\[\frac{r}{h}=\frac{R}{H} \Longrightarrow r=\frac{R}{H}h\]
The volume \(V(t)\) of the liquid in the cone and the surface area \(S(t)\) in contact with air at time \(t\) are:
\[V=\frac{1}{3}\pi r^{2}h=\frac{1}{3}\pi\left( \frac{R}{H}h \right)^{2}h=\frac{\pi R^{2}}{3H^{2}}h^{3},\quad S=\pi r^{2}=\frac{\pi R^{2}}{H^{2}}h^{2}\]
Differentiating \(V\) with respect to time \(t\):
\[\frac{dV}{dt}=\frac{\pi R^{2}}{3H^{2}} \cdot 3h^{2}\frac{dh}{dt}=\frac{\pi R^{2}}{H^{2}}h^{2}\frac{dh}{dt}=S\frac{dh}{dt}\]
According to the problem statement, the liquid evaporates at a rate proportional to \(S\) with constant \(k > 0\):
\[\frac{dV}{dt}= - kS \Longrightarrow S\frac{dh}{dt}= - kS \Longrightarrow \frac{dh}{dt}= - k\]
Integrating with respect to \(t\):
\[h(t)= - kt + C\]
At \(t=0\), \(h(0)=H \Longrightarrow C=H\), so \(h(t)=H - kt\). When the cone becomes completely empty, \(h(T)=0\):
\[H - kT=0 \Longrightarrow T=\frac{H}{k}\]

IIT200500001Q01:
Let the equilateral triangle be \(\triangle ABC\) with side length \(a\), and let the centres of the two coins touching side \(BC\) be \(O_{1}\) and \(O_{2}\), each of radius \(r = 1\text{ cm}\).
• Since the circle with centre \(O_{1}\) touches two sides meeting at vertex \(B\) (where \(\angle B = 60^{\circ}\)), the line \(BO_{1}\) bisects \(\angle B\), making an angle of \(30^{\circ}\) with side \(BC\).
• Dropping a perpendicular from \(O_{1}\) to \(BC\) at the point of tangency \(P_{1}\), we have \(O_{1}P_{1} = r = 1\text{ cm}\) and \(BP_{1} = r\cot 30^{\circ} = \sqrt{3}\text{ cm}\).
• The distance between the points of tangency \(P_{1}\) and \(P_{2}\) along \(BC\) is \(P_{1}P_{2} = O_{1}O_{2} = 2r = 2\text{ cm}\), and by symmetry \(P_{2}C = \sqrt{3}\text{ cm}\).
• Thus, the side length of the equilateral triangle is \(a = \sqrt{3} + 2 + \sqrt{3} = 2 + 2\sqrt{3}\text{ cm}\), and its area is:
\[\text{Area} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}a^{2} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}\left( 2 + 2\sqrt{3} \right)^{2} = \sqrt{3}\left( 4 + 2\sqrt{3} \right) = 6 + 4\sqrt{3}{\text{ cm}}^{2}\]
IIT200500001Q02:
The curves \(y = (x - 1)^{2}\) and \(y = (x + 1)^{2}\) are symmetric about the y-axis and intersect at \((0,1)\). For \(x \geq 0\), setting \((x - 1)^{2} = \frac{1}{4}\) on the inner branch gives \(x = \frac{1}{2}\). By symmetry:
\[\text{Area} = 2\int_{0}^{1/2}{}\left[ (x - 1)^{2} - \frac{1}{4} \right] dx = 2\left[ \frac{(x - 1)^{3}}{3} - \frac{x}{4} \right]_{0}^{1/2} = 2\left[ \left( - \frac{1}{24} - \frac{1}{8} \right) - \left( - \frac{1}{3} \right) \right] = \frac{1}{3}\]
IIT200500001Q03:
Rewriting \(x^{3} + 3x^{2} + 3x + 3 = (x + 1)^{3} + 2\) and substituting \(t = x + 1\):
\[I = \int_{- 1}^{1}{}\left( t^{3} + 2 + t\cos t \right)dt = 0 + \int_{- 1}^{1}{}2\ dt + 0 = 4\]
(since \(t^{3}\) and \(t\cos t\) are odd functions on \([ - 1,1]\)).
IIT200500001Q04:
The tangent to \(x^{2} = y - 6\) at \((1,7)\) is \(x(1) = \frac{y + 7}{2} - 6 \Longrightarrow 2x - y + 5 = 0\). The point of contact \(P(h,k)\) is the foot of the perpendicular from the circle's centre \(C( - 8, - 6)\) onto \(2x - y + 5 = 0\):
\[\frac{h + 8}{2} = \frac{k + 6}{- 1} = - \frac{2( - 8) - ( - 6) + 5}{2^{2} + ( - 1)^{2}} = 1 \Longrightarrow (h,k) = ( - 6, - 7)\]
IIT200500001Q05:
Writing \(\frac{dx}{dy} = \frac{x}{y} + \frac{y}{x}\) and putting \(x = vy \Longrightarrow \frac{dx}{dy} = v + y\frac{dv}{dy}\):
\[y\frac{dv}{dy} = \frac{1}{v} \Longrightarrow \int_{}^{}{}v\ dv = \int_{}^{}{}\frac{dy}{y} \Longrightarrow \frac{x^{2}}{2y^{2}} = \ln|y| + C\]
Using \(y(1) = 1 \Longrightarrow C = \frac{1}{2}\). For \(y(x_{0}) = e\):
\[\frac{x_{0}^{2}}{2e^{2}} = \ln e + \frac{1}{2} = \frac{3}{2} \Longrightarrow x_{0} = \pm e\sqrt{3}\]
IIT200500001Q06:
Let the centre be \((h,k)\), so its radius is \(|k|\). Since it touches \(x^{2} + (y - 1)^{2} = 1\) externally:
\[\sqrt{h^{2} + (k - 1)^{2}} = |k| + 1 \Longrightarrow h^{2} + k^{2} - 2k + 1 = k^{2} + 2|k| + 1 \Longrightarrow h^{2} = 2(k + |k|)\]
For \(k \geq 0\), \(h^{2} = 4k\); for \(k < 0\), \(h = 0\). Hence the locus is \(\{ x^{2} = 4y\} \cup \{(0,y),y < 0\}\).
IIT200500001Q07:
Differentiating both sides with respect to \(x\) via Leibniz's rule:
\[- \sin^{2}x \cdot f(\sin x)\cos x = - \cos x \Longrightarrow f(t) = \frac{1}{t^{2}} \Longrightarrow f\left( \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \right) = 3\]
IIT200500001Q09:
The centroid of \(\triangle ABC\) is \((x,y,z) = \left( \frac{a}{3},\frac{b}{3},\frac{c}{3} \right)\). Since the plane is at a unit distance from the origin:
\[\frac{1}{a^{2}} + \frac{1}{b^{2}} + \frac{1}{c^{2}} = 1 \Longrightarrow \frac{1}{9x^{2}} + \frac{1}{9y^{2}} + \frac{1}{9z^{2}} = 1 \Longrightarrow \frac{1}{x^{2}} + \frac{1}{y^{2}} + \frac{1}{z^{2}} = 9 \Longrightarrow K = 9\]
IIT200500001Q10:
Since \(\alpha + \beta\), \(\alpha^{2} + \beta^{2}\), and \(\alpha^{3} + \beta^{3}\) are in G.P. (Tardigrade Q10 (https://tardigrade.in/question/let-f-x-ax-2-bx-c-a-not-equal-0-and-delta-b-2-4ac-if-a-beta-9xyltvwm)):
\[\left( \alpha^{2} + \beta^{2} \right)^{2} = (\alpha + \beta)\left( \alpha^{3} + \beta^{3} \right) \Longrightarrow \alpha\beta(\alpha - \beta)^{2} = 0 \Longrightarrow \left( \frac{c}{a} \right)\left( \frac{\Delta}{a^{2}} \right) = 0 \Longrightarrow c\Delta = 0\]
IIT200500001Q11:
The tangent at \((a\cos\theta,b\sin\theta)\) is \(\frac{x\cos\theta}{a} + \frac{y\sin\theta}{b} = 1\), with intercepts \(OA = \frac{a}{\cos\theta}\) and \(OB = \frac{b}{\sin\theta}\):
\[\text{Area}( \triangle OAB) = \frac{1}{2}|OA \cdot OB| = \frac{ab}{|\sin 2\theta|} \geq ab\]
IIT200500001Q13:
\[x\ dy - y\ dx = y^{2}\ dy \Longrightarrow - d\left( \frac{x}{y} \right) = dy \Longrightarrow - \frac{x}{y} = y + C\]
Using \(y(1) = 1 \Longrightarrow C = - 2 \Longrightarrow y^{2} - 2y + x = 0\). For \(x = - 3\), \(y^{2} - 2y - 3 = 0 \Longrightarrow y = 3\) (since \(y > 0\)).

IIT200500001Q23: By Cayley--Hamilton Theorem, \(\det(A - \lambda I) = (1 - \lambda)(\lambda^{2} - 5\lambda + 6) = 0 \Longrightarrow A^{3} - 6A^{2} + 11A - 6I = O \Longrightarrow 6A^{- 1} = A^{2} - 6A + 11I \Longrightarrow (c,d) = ( - 6,11)\).
IIT200500001Q24:
By Mollweide's formula (Tardigrade Q24 (https://tardigrade.in/question/in-a-triangle-abc-among-the-following-which-one-is-true-yqsb8bqy)):
\[\frac{b - c}{a} = \frac{\sin B - \sin C}{\sin A} = \frac{2\cos\frac{B + C}{2}\sin\frac{B - C}{2}}{2\sin\frac{A}{2}\cos\frac{A}{2}} = \frac{\sin\frac{B - C}{2}}{\cos\frac{A}{2}} \Longrightarrow (b - c)\cos\frac{A}{2} = a\sin\left( \frac{B - C}{2} \right)\]
IIT200500001Q25: By Gram--Schmidt orthogonalization, \({\overrightarrow{b}}_{1} \cdot \overrightarrow{a} = 0\), \({\overrightarrow{c}}_{2} \cdot \overrightarrow{a} = 0\), and \({\overrightarrow{c}}_{2} \cdot {\overrightarrow{b}}_{1} = 0\), so \(\left(\overrightarrow{a},{\overrightarrow{b}}_{1},{\overrightarrow{c}}_{2}\right)\) are mutually orthogonal.
IIT200500001Q26: At \(x = 0\), \(y(0) = \pi\). Differentiating once gives \(y'\cos x - y\sin x + \cos y - x\sin y \cdot y' = 0 \Longrightarrow y'(0) = 1\). Differentiating twice at \(x = 0\) gives \(y''(0) - \pi = 0 \Longrightarrow f''(0) = \pi\).
IIT200500001Q27: Let \(g(x) = f(x) - x^{2}\). Since \(g(1) = g(2) = g(3) = 0\), Rolle's Theorem on \([ 1,2]\) and \([ 2,3]\) gives \(c_{1} \in (1,2)\) and \(c_{2} \in (2,3)\) with \(g'(c_{1}) = g'(c_{2}) = 0\), and Rolle's Theorem on \([ c_{1},c_{2}]\) gives \(c \in (1,3)\) with \(g''(c) = 0 \Longrightarrow f''(c) = 2\).

IIT200500000Q01:
Let \(C,S,B,T\) be the events of the person going by car, scooter, bus, or train, respectively:
\[P(C) = \frac{1}{7},\quad P(S) = \frac{3}{7},\quad P(B) = \frac{2}{7},\quad P(T) = \frac{1}{7}\]
Let \(\overline{L}\) be the event of the person reaching the office in time. Then:
\[P\left(\overline{L}|C\right) = \frac{7}{9},\quad P\left(\overline{L}|S\right) = \frac{8}{9},\quad P\left(\overline{L}|B\right) = \frac{5}{9},\quad P\left(\overline{L}|T\right) = \frac{8}{9}\]
By Bayes' theorem:
\[P\left(C|\overline{L}\right) = \frac{P(C)P\left(\overline{L}|C\right)}{P\left(\overline{L}\right)} = \frac{\frac{1}{7} \times \frac{7}{9}}{\frac{1}{7} \times \frac{7}{9} + \frac{3}{7} \times \frac{8}{9} + \frac{2}{7} \times \frac{5}{9} + \frac{1}{7} \times \frac{8}{9}} = \frac{7}{7 + 24 + 10 + 8} = \frac{1}{7}\]
IIT200500000Q02:
Let \(y = 2\sin t\). Then:
\[y = \frac{1 - 2x + 5x^{2}}{3x^{2} - 2x - 1} \Longrightarrow (3y - 5)x^{2} - 2(y - 1)x - (y + 1) = 0\]
Since \(x \in {\mathbb{R}} \smallsetminus \left\{ 1, - \frac{1}{3} \right\}\), the discriminant \(D \geq 0\):
\[4(y - 1)^{2} + 4(3y - 5)(y + 1) \geq 0 \Longrightarrow y^{2} - y - 1 \geq 0\]
\[\Longrightarrow y \geq \frac{1 + \sqrt{5}}{2}\quad \text{ or }\quad y \leq \frac{1 - \sqrt{5}}{2}\]
\[\Longrightarrow \sin t \geq \frac{1 + \sqrt{5}}{4}\quad \text{ or }\quad \sin t \leq \frac{1 - \sqrt{5}}{4}\]
Hence, for \(t \in \left[ - \frac{\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2} \right]\), the range of \(t\) is:
\[t \in \left[ - \frac{\pi}{2}, - \frac{\pi}{10} \right] \cup \left[ \frac{3\pi}{10},\frac{\pi}{2} \right]\]

Let \(A,B,C\) be the centres of the three circles with radii \(3,4,5\). Then the sides of \(\triangle ABC\) are \(c = AB = 3 + 4 = 7\), \(a = BC = 4 + 5 = 9\), and \(b = CA = 5 + 3 = 8\).
Clearly, the point \(P\) (the radical centre where the common internal tangents meet) is the incentre of \(\triangle ABC\), and its distance from the points of contact equals the inradius \(r\) of \(\triangle ABC\):
\[2s = 7 + 8 + 9 = 24 \Longrightarrow s = 12\]
\[r = \frac{\Delta}{s} = \sqrt{\frac{(s - a)(s - b)(s - c)}{s}} = \sqrt{\frac{5 \cdot 4 \cdot 3}{12}} = \sqrt{5}\]

IIT200500000Q04:
Let the equation of the plane containing the given line be \((2x - y + z - 3) + \lambda(3x + y + z - 5) = 0\):
\[(3\lambda + 2)x + (\lambda - 1)y + (\lambda + 1)z - 5\lambda - 3 = 0\]
Since its distance from \((2,1, - 1)\) is \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\):
\[\left| \frac{6\lambda + 4 + \lambda - 1 - \lambda - 1 - 5\lambda - 3}{\sqrt{(3\lambda + 2)^{2} + (\lambda - 1)^{2} + (\lambda + 1)^{2}}} \right| = \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \Longrightarrow 6(\lambda - 1)^{2} = 11\lambda^{2} + 12\lambda + 6\]
\[\Longrightarrow 5\lambda^{2} + 24\lambda = 0 \Longrightarrow \lambda = 0\ \text{ or }\ \lambda = - \frac{24}{5}\]
Hence, the planes are \(2x - y + z - 3 = 0\) and \(62x + 29y + 19z - 105 = 0\).
IIT200500000Q05:
Dividing by \(|x_{1} - x_{2}|\) for \(x_{1} \neq x_{2}\) and taking the limit as \(x_{1} \to x_{2}\):
\[\lim\limits_{x_{1} \to x_{2}}\left| \frac{f(x_{1}) - f(x_{2})}{x_{1} - x_{2}} \right| \leq \lim\limits_{x_{1} \to x_{2}}|x_{1} - x_{2}| = 0 \Longrightarrow f'(x) = 0\quad \forall x \in {\mathbb{R}}\]
Hence \(f(x)\) is a constant function. Since \(P(1,2)\) lies on the curve, \(f(x) = 2\), and the equation of the tangent is \(y - 2 = 0\).
IIT200500000Q06:
Summing the arithmetico-geometric progression (AGP):
\[S_{n} = \sum_{k = 1}^{n}{}k \cdot 2^{n + 1 - k} = 2^{n + 1}\sum_{k = 1}^{n}{}k \cdot 2^{- k} = 2^{n + 1} \cdot 2\left[ 1 - \frac{1}{2^{n}} - \frac{n}{2^{n + 1}} \right] = 2\left( 2^{n + 1} - 2 - n \right)\]
Equating to \(\left( \frac{n + 1}{4} \right)(2^{n + 1} - n - 2)\):
\[\frac{n + 1}{4} = 2 \Longrightarrow n = 7\]

The lines \(y = x\) and \(x + y = 2\) are perpendicular and intersect at \(A(1,1)\). The horizontal line \(y = k\) through \(P(h,k)\) meets \(y = x\) at \(B(k,k)\) and \(x + y = 2\) at \(C(2 - k,k)\).
Thus \(AB = AC = \sqrt{2}|k - 1|\), and the area of \(\triangle ABC\) is:
\[\text{Area} = \frac{1}{2} \cdot AB \cdot AC = \frac{1}{2} \cdot 2(k - 1)^{2} = (k - 1)^{2} = 4h^{2} \Longrightarrow k - 1 = \pm 2h\]
Hence, the locus of \(P\) is \(y = 2x + 1\) or \(y = - 2x + 1\).

IIT200500000Q08:
Using \(\int_{0}^{2a}{}f(x)\ dx = \left\{ \begin{matrix} 0, & \text{ if }\ f(2a - x) = - f(x) \\ 2\int_{0}^{a}f(x)\ dx, & \text{ if }\ f(2a - x) = f(x) \end{matrix} \right.\):
\[I = 6\int_{0}^{\pi/2}{}e^{\cos x}\sin x\cos\left( \frac{1}{2}\cos x \right)dx\]
Putting \(\cos x = t \Longrightarrow - \sin x\ dx = dt\):
\[I = 6\int_{0}^{1}{}e^{t}\cos\left( \frac{t}{2} \right)dt = \frac{24}{5}\left( e\cos\frac{1}{2} + \frac{e}{2}\sin\frac{1}{2} - 1 \right)\]

IIT200500000Q09.t:

Since \(\hat{v}\) is the unit vector along the incident ray, \(\hat{w}\) is the unit vector along the reflected ray, and \(\hat{a}\) is the outward unit normal along the external bisector of \(\hat{v}\) and \(\hat{w}\):
\[\hat{w} - \hat{v} = \lambda\hat{a}\]
Squaring both sides, where \(2\theta\) is the angle between \(- \hat{v}\) and \(\hat{w}\) (or \(\hat{v}\) and \(\hat{w}\)):
\[|\hat{w} - \hat{v}|^{2} = \lambda^{2} \Longrightarrow 1 + 1 - 2\hat{w} \cdot \hat{v} = \lambda^{2} \Longrightarrow 2 - 2\cos 2\theta = \lambda^{2} \Longrightarrow \lambda = 2\sin\theta = 2\cos(90^{\circ} - \theta) = - 2\left(\hat{a} \cdot \hat{v}\right)\]
\[\Longrightarrow \hat{w} = \hat{v} - 2\left(\hat{a} \cdot \hat{v}\right)\hat{a}\]

IIT200500000Q10:
Any point on the hyperbola \(\frac{x^{2}}{9} - \frac{y^{2}}{4} = 1\) is \((3\sec\theta,2\tan\theta)\). Its chord of contact with respect to \(x^{2} + y^{2} = 9\) is:
\[3x\sec\theta + 2y\tan\theta = 9\]
If \((x_{1},y_{1})\) is the midpoint of the chord of contact, its equation is also \(xx_{1} + yy_{1} = x_{1}^{2} + y_{1}^{2}\). Comparing coefficients:
\[\frac{3\sec\theta}{x_{1}} = \frac{2\tan\theta}{y_{1}} = \frac{9}{x_{1}^{2} + y_{1}^{2}} \Longrightarrow \sec\theta = \frac{3x_{1}}{x_{1}^{2} + y_{1}^{2}},\quad \tan\theta = \frac{9y_{1}}{2(x_{1}^{2} + y_{1}^{2})}\]
Using \(\sec^{2}\theta - \tan^{2}\theta = 1\), the required locus is:
\[\frac{x^{2}}{9} - \frac{y^{2}}{4} = \left( \frac{x^{2} + y^{2}}{9} \right)^{2}\]
IIT200500000Q11:
Equating the tangency conditions \(y = mx + 4\sqrt{1 + m^{2}}\) and \(y = mx + \sqrt{25m^{2} + 4}\):
\[16(1 + m^{2}) = 25m^{2} + 4 \Longrightarrow 9m^{2} = 12 \Longrightarrow m = \pm \frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\]
Since the tangent touches in the first quadrant, \(m = - \frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\), and the common tangent is:
\[y = - \frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}x + 4\sqrt{\frac{7}{3}}\]
It meets the coordinate axes at \(A\left(2\sqrt{7},0\right)\) and \(B\left( 0,4\sqrt{\frac{7}{3}} \right)\), so the intercept length is:
\[AB = \sqrt{28 + \frac{112}{3}} = \frac{14}{\sqrt{3}}\]
IIT200500000Q12:
\[Length\ of\ tangent = \left| y\sqrt{1 + \left( \frac{dx}{dy} \right)^{2}} \right| = 1 \Longrightarrow \frac{dy}{dx} = \pm \frac{y}{\sqrt{1 - y^{2}}} \Longrightarrow \int_{}^{}{}\frac{\sqrt{1 - y^{2}}}{y}\ dy = \pm x + c\]
Substituting \(y = \sin\theta\), \(dy = \cos\theta\ d\theta\) and integrating gives:
\[\sqrt{1 - y^{2}} + \ln\left| \frac{1 - \sqrt{1 - y^{2}}}{y} \right| = \pm x + c\]

The centre of the circle \(z_{0} = 1\) is the midpoint of the diagonals of the square, and \(z_{1} = 2 + \sqrt{3}i\):
\[\frac{z_{1} + z_{2}}{2} = z_{0} \Longrightarrow z_{2} = 2(1) - \left(2 + \sqrt{3}i\right) = - \sqrt{3}i\]
\[\frac{z_{3,4} - 1}{z_{1} - 1} = e^{\pm i\pi/2} = \pm i \Longrightarrow z_{3},z_{4} = 1 \pm i\left(1 + \sqrt{3}i\right) = \left(1 - \sqrt{3}\right) + i\ \text{ and }\ \left(1 + \sqrt{3}\right) - i\]

IIT200500000Q15:
Putting \(x = y\) in \(f(x - y) = f(x)g(y) - f(y)g(x)\) gives \(f(0) = 0\). Putting \(y = 0\) gives \(g(0) = 1\), and \(f( - h) = - f(h)\).
Thus \(f'(0^{+}) = \lim\limits_{h \to 0^{+}}\frac{f(h)}{h} = \lim\limits_{h \to 0^{+}}\frac{f( - h)}{- h} = f'(0^{-})\), so \(f(x)\) is differentiable at \(x = 0\).
Putting \(y = x\) in \(g(x - y) = g(x)g(y) + f(x)f(y)\) gives:
\[f^{2}(x) + g^{2}(x) = g(0) = 1 \Longrightarrow 2g(0)g'(0) = - 2f(0)f'(0) = 0 \Longrightarrow g'(0) = 0\]
IIT200500000Q16:
Let \(P(x) = ax^{3} + bx^{2} + cx + d\). From the given conditions:
\[P( - 1) = - a + b - c + d = 10,\quad P(1) = a + b + c + d = - 6\]
\[P'( - 1) = 3a - 2b + c = 0,\quad P''(1) = 6a + 2b = 0 \Longrightarrow b = - 3a\]
Solving for \(a,b,c,d\) gives \(a = 1,b = - 3,c = - 9,d = 5\), so:
\[P(x) = x^{3} - 3x^{2} - 9x + 5,\quad P'(x) = 3(x + 1)(x - 3)\]
Thus \(x = - 1\) gives the local maximum \(( - 1,10)\) and \(x = 3\) gives the local minimum \((3, - 22)\). The distance between them is:
\[\sqrt{(3 - ( - 1))^{2} + ( - 22 - 10)^{2}} = \sqrt{16 + 1024} = 4\sqrt{65}\ \text{units}\]

IIT200500000Q17.t:
From \(f'(x) = g(x)\) and \(|f(x)| \leq 1\):
\[\left| \int_{0}^{3}{}g(x)\ dx \right| = |f(3) - f(0)| \leq 2\quad \text{ and }\quad \left| \int_{- 3}^{0}{}g(x)\ dx \right| = |f(0) - f( - 3)| \leq 2\]
\[\Longrightarrow \left| \int_{0}^{3}{}g(x)\ dx \right| + \left| \int_{- 3}^{0}{}g(x)\ dx \right| \leq 4\quad \ldots(1)\]
Also, from \(f^{2}(0) + g^{2}(0) = 9\) and \(|f(0)| \leq 1\), we have \(2\sqrt{2} \leq |g(0)| \leq 3\).
{{figure}}
• Case I (\(2\sqrt{2} \leq g(0) \leq 3\)): Suppose \(g(x)\) is concave upward (\(g''(x) > 0\)) for all \(x \in ( - 3,3)\) and \(g(x) > 0\). Then the tangent line to \(y = g(x)\) at \((0,g(0))\) lies below the curve, so the sum of areas satisfies:
\[\left| \int_{- 3}^{0}{}g(x)\ dx \right| + \left| \int_{0}^{3}{}g(x)\ dx \right| \geq 6g(0) \geq 12\sqrt{2} > 4\]
(or at least \(3g(0) \geq 6\sqrt{2} > 4\) on one of the half-intervals \([ - 3,0]\) or \([ 0,3]\) depending on the sign of \(g'(0)\)), which contradicts \((1)\). Hence \(g''(c) < 0\) at some point \(c \in ( - 3,3)\) where \(g(c) \geq 2\sqrt{2} > 0\), giving \(g(c)g''(c) < 0\).
• Case II (\(- 3 \leq g(0) \leq - 2\sqrt{2}\)): Similarly, if \(g(x)\) were concave downward (\(g''(x) < 0\)) across the region where \(g(x) < 0\), then \(\left| \int_{- 3}^{0}{}g(x)\ dx \right| + \left| \int_{0}^{3}{}g(x)\ dx \right| > 6\sqrt{2} > 4\), contradicting \((1)\). Thus \(g''(c) > 0\) at some point \(c \in ( - 3,3)\) where \(g(c) \leq - 2\sqrt{2} < 0\), so \(g(c)g''(c) < 0\).
Hence, there exists \(c \in ( - 3,3)\) such that \(g(c)g''(c) < 0\).

IIT200200000Q01:
Step 1: Analyze the Arithmetic Progression (\(a,A_{1},A_{2},b\) in A.P.)
Since \(a,A_{1},A_{2},b\) are in A.P. with common difference \(d=\frac{b-a}{3}\), the sum of the two arithmetic means is equal to the sum of the extremes:
\[A_{1}+A_{2}=a+b\quad (\text{Equation} 1)\]
Step 2: Analyze the Geometric Progression (\(a,G_{1},G_{2},b\) in G.P.)
Since \(a,G_{1},G_{2},b\) are positive real numbers in G.P. with common ratio \(r=\left( \frac{b}{a} \right)^{\frac{1}{3}}\), the product of the two geometric means equals the product of the extremes:
\[G_{1}G_{2}=ab\quad (\text{Equation} 2)\]
Step 3: Analyze the Harmonic Progression (\(a,H_{1},H_{2},b\) in H.P.)
Since \(a,H_{1},H_{2},b\) are in H.P., their reciprocals \(\frac{1}{a},\frac{1}{H_{1}},\frac{1}{H_{2}},\frac{1}{b}\) form an A.P. with common difference \(D\):
\[D=\frac{\frac{1}{b}-\frac{1}{a}}{3}=\frac{a-b}{3ab}\]
Therefore, the reciprocals of \(H_{1}\) and \(H_{2}\) are:
\[\frac{1}{H_{1}}=\frac{1}{a}+\frac{a-b}{3ab}=\frac{a+2b}{3ab} \Longrightarrow H_{1}=\frac{3ab}{a+2b}\]
\[\frac{1}{H_{2}}=\frac{1}{a}+\frac{2\left( a-b \right)}{3ab}=\frac{2a+b}{3ab} \Longrightarrow H_{2}=\frac{3ab}{2a+b}\]
Also, by the sum property of the reciprocal A.P., we have:
\[\frac{1}{H_{1}}+\frac{1}{H_{2}}=\frac{1}{a}+\frac{1}{b} \Longrightarrow \frac{H_{1}+H_{2}}{H_{1}H_{2}}=\frac{a+b}{ab}\quad (\text{Equation} 3)\]
Step 4: Combine the Relations to Establish the Required Equality
Substituting \(a+b=A_{1}+A_{2}\) from Equation (1) and \(ab=G_{1}G_{2}\) from Equation (2) into Equation (3):
\[\frac{H_{1}+H_{2}}{H_{1}H_{2}}=\frac{A_{1}+A_{2}}{G_{1}G_{2}} \Longrightarrow \frac{G_{1}G_{2}}{H_{1}H_{2}}=\frac{A_{1}+A_{2}}{H_{1}+H_{2}}\]
Now compute the product \(H_{1}H_{2}\) explicitly from Step 3:
\[H_{1}H_{2}=\left( \frac{3ab}{a+2b} \right)\left( \frac{3ab}{2a+b} \right)=\frac{9a^{2}b^{2}}{\left( 2a+b \right)\left( a+2b \right)}\]
Dividing \(G_{1}G_{2}=ab\) by \(H_{1}H_{2}\) gives:
\[\frac{G_{1}G_{2}}{H_{1}H_{2}}=\frac{ab}{\frac{9a^{2}b^{2}}{\left( 2a+b \right)\left( a+2b \right)}}=\frac{\left( 2a+b \right)\left( a+2b \right)}{9ab}\]
Conclusion: Hence, \(\frac{G_{1}G_{2}}{H_{1}H_{2}}=\frac{A_{1}+A_{2}}{H_{1}+H_{2}}=\frac{\left( 2a+b \right)\left( a+2b \right)}{9ab}\). (Hence Proved)
IIT200200000Q02:
Step 1: Formulate the Inductive Proposition \(P(n)\)
Let \(P(n)\) be the statement that \(f(n)=(25)^{n+1}-24n+5735\) is divisible by \((24)^{2}=576\), where \(n \in {\mathbb{N}}\).
Step 2: Base Case (\(n=1\))
Evaluating \(f(1)\) for \(n=1\):
\[f(1)=(25)^{1+1}-24(1)+5735=625-24+5735=6336\]
Factoring \(6336\) with respect to \((24)^{2}=576\):
\[6336=11 \times 576=11 \times (24)^{2}\]
Since \(f(1)\) is an exact integer multiple of \((24)^{2}\), the statement \(P(1)\) holds true.
Step 3: Inductive Hypothesis (\(n=k\))
Assume that \(P(k)\) holds true for some positive integer \(k \geq 1\). That is, there exists an integer \(m \in {\mathbb{Z}}\) such that:
\[(25)^{k+1}-24k+5735=576m \Longrightarrow (25)^{k+1}=576m+24k-5735\quad (\text{Equation} 1)\]
Step 4: Inductive Step (\(n=k+1\))
Consider \(f\left( k+1 \right)\):
\[f\left( k+1 \right)=(25)^{\left( k+1 \right)+1}-24\left( k+1 \right)+5735=25 \cdot (25)^{k+1}-24k-24+5735\]
Substitute the expression for \((25)^{k+1}\) from Equation (1):
\[f\left( k+1 \right)=25\left( 576m+24k-5735 \right)-24k+5711\]
\[f\left( k+1 \right)=25 \times 576m+\left( 25 \times 24-24 \right)k-143375+5711\]
\[f\left( k+1 \right)=25 \times 576m+24(24)k-137664\]
Since \(24 \times 24=576=(24)^{2}\) and \(137664=239 \times 576=239 \times (24)^{2}\), we factor out \((24)^{2}\):
\[f\left( k+1 \right)=(24)^{2}\left( 25m+k-239 \right)\]
Since \(m,k \in {\mathbb{Z}}\), the quantity \(\left( 25m+k-239 \right)\) is an integer, so \(f\left( k+1 \right)\) is divisible by \((24)^{2}\). Thus \(P(k) \Longrightarrow P\left( k+1 \right)\).
Conclusion: By the Principle of Mathematical Induction, \((25)^{n+1}-24n+5735\) is divisible by \((24)^{2}\) for all \(n=1,2,3,\ldots\) (Hence Proved)
IIT200200000Q03:
Step 1: Simplify the Inner Expression \(\sin \left( \cot^{-1}x \right)\)
Let \(\theta=\cot^{-1}x\) for any real number \(x \in {\mathbb{R}}\). By definition of the principal value branch, \(\theta \in (0,\pi)\) and \(\cot \theta=x\).
Since \(\theta \in (0,\pi)\), \(\sin \theta>0\). Using the Pythagorean identity \(\csc^{2}\theta=1+\cot^{2}\theta\):
\[\sin \theta=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+\cot^{2}\theta}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{x^{2}+1}} \Longrightarrow \sin \left( \cot^{-1}x \right)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{x^{2}+1}}\]
Step 2: Simplify the Outer Expression \(\cos \left( \tan^{-1}\left( \sin \theta \right) \right)\)
Substitute \(\sin \left( \cot^{-1}x \right)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{x^{2}+1}}\) into the given left-hand side (LHS):
\[\text{LHS}=\cos \left( \tan^{-1}\left( \frac{1}{\sqrt{x^{2}+1}} \right) \right)\]
Let \(\phi=\tan^{-1}\left( \frac{1}{\sqrt{x^{2}+1}} \right)\). Since \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{x^{2}+1}}>0\), we have \(\phi \in \left( 0,\frac{\pi}{2} \right)\), where \(\tan \phi=\frac{1}{\sqrt{x^{2}+1}}\) and \(\cos \phi>0\).
Using the identity \(\sec^{2}\phi=1+\tan^{2}\phi\):
\[\sec^{2}\phi=1+\left( \frac{1}{\sqrt{x^{2}+1}} \right)^{2}=1+\frac{1}{x^{2}+1}=\frac{x^{2}+2}{x^{2}+1}\]
Taking the reciprocal and positive square root for \(\cos \phi\):
\[\text{LHS}=\cos \phi=\frac{1}{\sec \phi}=\sqrt{\frac{x^{2}+1}{x^{2}+2}}=\text{RHS}\]
Conclusion: Therefore, \(\cos \tan^{-1}\sin \cot^{-1}x=\sqrt{\frac{x^{2}+1}{x^{2}+2}}\) for all \(x \in {\mathbb{R}}\). (Hence Proved)
IIT200200000Q04:
Step 1: Define the Events and Prior Probabilities
Let \(E_{1}\) be the event that the randomly drawn coin is fair, and \(E_{2}\) be the event that the drawn coin is biased.
Since the box contains \(N\) coins in total, of which \(m\) are fair and \(\left( N-m \right)\) are biased:
\[P\left( E_{1} \right)=\frac{m}{N},\quad P\left( E_{2} \right)=\frac{N-m}{N}\]
Step 2: Compute Likelihoods of the Observed Outcome \(A=(H,T)\)
Let \(A\) be the event that in two independent tosses of the selected coin, the first toss results in Head (\(H\)) and the second toss results in Tail (\(T\)).
• If the coin is fair (\(E_{1}\)): \(P\left( H \middle| E_{1} \right)=\frac{1}{2}\) and \(P\left( T \middle| E_{1} \right)=1-\frac{1}{2}=\frac{1}{2}\). By independence of tosses:
\[P\left( A \middle| E_{1} \right)=\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{2}=\frac{1}{4}\]
• If the coin is biased (\(E_{2}\)): \(P\left( H \middle| E_{2} \right)=\frac{2}{3}\) and \(P\left( T \middle| E_{2} \right)=1-\frac{2}{3}=\frac{1}{3}\). By independence of tosses:
\[P\left( A \middle| E_{2} \right)=\frac{2}{3} \times \frac{1}{3}=\frac{2}{9}\]
Step 3: Apply Bayes' Theorem
By Bayes' Theorem, the conditional probability that the drawn coin is fair given that event \(A\) occurred is:
\[P\left( E_{1} \middle| A \right)=\frac{P\left( E_{1} \right) \cdot P\left( A \middle| E_{1} \right)}{P\left( E_{1} \right) \cdot P\left( A \middle| E_{1} \right)+P\left( E_{2} \right) \cdot P\left( A \middle| E_{2} \right)}\]
Substitute the values from Steps 1 and 2:
\[P\left( E_{1} \middle| A \right)=\frac{\frac{m}{N} \cdot \frac{1}{4}}{\frac{m}{N} \cdot \frac{1}{4}+\frac{N-m}{N} \cdot \frac{2}{9}}=\frac{\frac{m}{4}}{\frac{m}{4}+\frac{2\left( N-m \right)}{9}}\]
Multiplying the numerator and denominator by \(36\):
\[P\left( E_{1} \middle| A \right)=\frac{9m}{9m+8\left( N-m \right)}=\frac{9m}{8N+m}\]
Final Answer: The probability that the coin drawn is fair is \(\frac{9m}{8N+m}\).
IIT200200000Q05:
Step 1: Factorize the Given Polynomial Equation
Grouping terms in the given equation \(z^{p+q}-z^{p}-z^{q}+1=0\):
\[z^{p}\left( z^{q}-1 \right)-1\left( z^{q}-1 \right)=0 \Longrightarrow \left( z^{p}-1 \right)\left( z^{q}-1 \right)=0\]
Using the cyclotomic factorization \(z^{n}-1=\left( z-1 \right)\left( 1+z+z^{2}+\ldots+z^{n-1} \right)\), we obtain:
\[\left( z-1 \right)^{2}\left( 1+z+z^{2}+\ldots+z^{p-1} \right)\left( 1+z+z^{2}+\ldots+z^{q-1} \right)=0\]
Step 2: Show That at Least One Sum Equals Zero
Since \(z=\alpha\) is a root of the equation and \(\alpha \neq 1\) (so \(\alpha-1 \neq 0\)), we can divide by \(\left( \alpha-1 \right)^{2} \neq 0\) to get:
\[\left( 1+\alpha+\alpha^{2}+\ldots+\alpha^{p-1} \right)\left( 1+\alpha+\alpha^{2}+\ldots+\alpha^{q-1} \right)=0\]
Therefore, at least one of the two factors must be zero: either \(1+\alpha+\alpha^{2}+\ldots+\alpha^{p-1}=0\) or \(1+\alpha+\alpha^{2}+\ldots+\alpha^{q-1}=0\).
Step 3: Prove That Both Cannot Vanish Simultaneously
Suppose, by contradiction, that both sums vanish simultaneously for the same \(\alpha \neq 1\):
\[1+\alpha+\alpha^{2}+\ldots+\alpha^{p-1}=0\quad \text{ and }\quad 1+\alpha+\alpha^{2}+\ldots+\alpha^{q-1}=0\]
Multiplying each equation by \(\left( \alpha-1 \right)\) yields:
\[\alpha^{p}-1=0 \Longrightarrow \alpha^{p}=1,\quad \text{ and }\quad \alpha^{q}-1=0 \Longrightarrow \alpha^{q}=1\]
Since \(p\) and \(q\) are distinct prime numbers, their greatest common divisor is \(\text{gcd}(p,q)=1\). By Bézout's identity, there exist integers \(u,v \in {\mathbb{Z}}\) such that \(pu+qv=1\). Consequently:
\[\alpha=\alpha^{1}=\alpha^{pu+qv}=\left( \alpha^{p} \right)^{u} \cdot \left( \alpha^{q} \right)^{v}=(1)^{u} \cdot (1)^{v}=1\]
This contradicts the given condition that \(\alpha \neq 1\). (Alternatively, \(\alpha=e^{i2k\pi/p}=e^{i2m\pi/q}\) implies \(kq=mp\), which forces \(k=m=0\) and \(\alpha=1\) since \(p,q\) are distinct primes.)
Conclusion: Either \(1+\alpha+\alpha^{2}+\ldots+\alpha^{p-1}=0\) or \(1+\alpha+\alpha^{2}+\ldots+\alpha^{q-1}=0\), but not both together. (Hence Proved)

IIT200200000Q06.t:

Step 1: Parametrize the Line \(L\) and Find Coordinates of \(P\) and \(Q\)
Let the variable straight line \(L\) passing through the origin \(O(0,0)\) have equation \(y=mx\) (where \(m \neq -1\) so that \(L\) intersects \(x+y=1\) and \(x+y=3\)).
• Coordinates of \(P\) (intersection of \(y=mx\) and \(x+y=1\)):
\[x+mx=1 \Longrightarrow x=\frac{1}{1+m},\quad y=\frac{m}{1+m} \Longrightarrow P=\left( \frac{1}{1+m},\frac{m}{1+m} \right)\]
• Coordinates of \(Q\) (intersection of \(y=mx\) and \(x+y=3\)):
\[x+mx=3 \Longrightarrow x=\frac{3}{1+m},\quad y=\frac{3m}{1+m} \Longrightarrow Q=\left( \frac{3}{1+m},\frac{3m}{1+m} \right)\]
Step 2: Write the Equations of Straight Lines \(L_{1}\) and \(L_{2}\)
• Line \(L_{1}\) passes through \(P\) and is parallel to \(2x-y=5\) (so its left-hand side is \(2x-y\)):
\[2x-y=2\left( \frac{1}{1+m} \right)-\frac{m}{1+m}=\frac{2-m}{1+m}=\frac{3-\left( 1+m \right)}{1+m}=\frac{3}{1+m}-1\quad (\text{Equation} 1)\]
• Line \(L_{2}\) passes through \(Q\) and is parallel to \(3x+y=5\) (so its left-hand side is \(3x+y\)):
\[3x+y=3\left( \frac{3}{1+m} \right)+\frac{3m}{1+m}=\frac{9+3m}{1+m}=\frac{6+3\left( 1+m \right)}{1+m}=\frac{6}{1+m}+3\quad (\text{Equation} 2)\]
Step 3: Eliminate Parameter \(m\) to Obtain the Locus of \(R(h,k)\)
Let \(R(h,k)\) be the point of intersection of \(L_{1}\) and \(L_{2}\). From Equations (1) and (2) evaluated at \((h,k)\):
\[\frac{3}{1+m}=2h-k+1\quad \text{ and }\quad \frac{6}{1+m}=3h+k-3\]
Substituting \(\frac{6}{1+m}=2\left( \frac{3}{1+m} \right)\) yields:
\[2\left( 2h-k+1 \right)=3h+k-3 \Longrightarrow 4h-2k+2=3h+k-3 \Longrightarrow h-3k+5=0\]
Replacing \((h,k)\) with general coordinates \((x,y)\), we obtain the linear equation \(x-3y+5=0\).
Conclusion: The locus of point \(R\), as \(L\) varies, is the straight line \(x-3y+5=0\). (Hence Proved)

IIT200200000Q07.t:

Step 1: Express the Equation of Line \(L\) and Find Intercepts \(OP\) and \(OQ\)
Let the slope of the line \(L\) be \(m=-k\), where \(k>0\) (since \(L\) has negative slope). The equation of \(L\) passing through \((8,2)\) is:
\[y-2=-k\left( x-8 \right)\]
• x-intercept \(P\) (setting \(y=0\)): \(-2=-k\left( x-8 \right) \Longrightarrow x=8+\frac{2}{k}\), so \(P=\left( 8+\frac{2}{k},0 \right)\) and \(OP=8+\frac{2}{k}\).
• y-intercept \(Q\) (setting \(x=0\)): \(y-2=8k \Longrightarrow y=2+8k\), so \(Q=\left( 0,2+8k \right)\) and \(OQ=2+8k\).
Since \(k>0\), both \(OP>0\) and \(OQ>0\), confirming that \(L\) cuts the positive coordinate axes.
Step 2: Minimize \(OP+OQ\) Using the AM--GM Inequality
Adding the two intercept lengths gives:
\[OP+OQ=\left( 8+\frac{2}{k} \right)+\left( 2+8k \right)=10+\left( 8k+\frac{2}{k} \right)\]
Since \(k>0\), both \(8k>0\) and \(\frac{2}{k}>0\). Applying the Arithmetic Mean--Geometric Mean (AM--GM) inequality:
\[\frac{8k+\frac{2}{k}}{2} \geq \sqrt{(8k) \cdot \left( \frac{2}{k} \right)}=\sqrt{16}=4 \Longrightarrow 8k+\frac{2}{k} \geq 8\]
Equality holds if and only if \(8k=\frac{2}{k} \Longrightarrow k^{2}=\frac{1}{4} \Longrightarrow k=\frac{1}{2}\) (so slope \(m=-\frac{1}{2}\), giving \(OP=12\) and \(OQ=6\)).
Therefore:
\[OP+OQ \geq 10+8=18\]
Final Answer: The absolute minimum value of \(OP+OQ\) is \(18\).

IIT200200000Q08.t:
{{figure}}
Step 1: Equation of the Ellipse and Tangent at Point of Contact \(P\)
Consider the standard ellipse centered at the origin \(C(0,0)\) with eccentricity \(e \in (0,1)\) and \(b^{2}=a^{2}\left( 1-e^{2} \right)\):
\[\frac{x^{2}}{a^{2}}+\frac{y^{2}}{b^{2}}=1\]
Consider the focus \(S(ae,0)\), whose corresponding directrix is \(x=\frac{a}{e}\). Let \(P\left( a\cos \theta,b\sin \theta \right)\) be any point on the ellipse. The equation of the tangent at \(P\) is:
\[\frac{x\cos \theta}{a}+\frac{y\sin \theta}{b}=1\quad \text{(Slope of tangent }m_{T}=-\frac{b\cos \theta}{a\sin \theta})\]
Step 2: Equation of the Perpendicular from Focus \(S(ae,0)\) to the Tangent
A line perpendicular to the tangent has slope \(m_{\bot}=\frac{a\sin \theta}{b\cos \theta}\). Since it passes through the focus \(S(ae,0)\), its equation is:
\[y-0=\frac{a\sin \theta}{b\cos \theta}\left( x-ae \right)\quad (\text{Equation} 1)\]
Step 3: Equation of the Line Joining Centre \(C(0,0)\) to \(P\left( a\cos \theta,b\sin \theta \right)\)
The straight line \(CP\) joining the centre \((0,0)\) to the point of contact \(\left( a\cos \theta,b\sin \theta \right)\) has equation:
\[y=\frac{b\sin \theta}{a\cos \theta}x\quad (\text{Equation} 2)\]
Step 4: Find the Point of Intersection of the Two Lines
Equating \(y\) from Equations (1) and (2) to find the \(x\)-coordinate of their intersection (for \(\sin \theta \neq 0,\cos \theta \neq 0\); if \(\sin \theta=0\), both lines coincide with the major axis \(y=0\) and meet the directrix at \(\left( \frac{a}{e},0 \right)\)):
\[\frac{a\sin \theta}{b\cos \theta}\left( x-ae \right)=\frac{b\sin \theta}{a\cos \theta}x \Longrightarrow a^{2}\left( x-ae \right)=b^{2}x\]
Substitute the fundamental eccentricity relation \(b^{2}=a^{2}\left( 1-e^{2} \right)\):
\[a^{2}x-a^{3}e=a^{2}\left( 1-e^{2} \right)x=a^{2}x-a^{2}e^{2}x \Longrightarrow a^{2}e^{2}x=a^{3}e \Longrightarrow x=\frac{a}{e}\]
(By identical symmetry, for the second focus \(S^{\prime}\left( -ae,0 \right)\), replacing \(e\) with \(-e\) gives \(x=-\frac{a}{e}\), which is the directrix corresponding to \(S^{\prime}\).)
Conclusion: Since the \(x\)-coordinate of the point of intersection is \(x=\frac{a}{e}\), the perpendicular from the focus upon any tangent and the central line \(CP\) always meet on the corresponding directrix. (Hence Proved)

IIT200200000Q09.t:
{{figure}}
Step 1: Analyze the Piecewise Curve and Points of Intersection for \(x \geq 1\)
In the region \(x \geq 1\), the curve \(y=\left| 2-x^{2} \right|\) splits at \(x=\sqrt{2}\) into two branches:
\(\left| 2-x^{2} \right|=\left\{ \begin{matrix} 2-x^{2}, & \text{if }1 \leq x \leq \sqrt{2} \\ x^{2}-2, & \text{if }x \geq \sqrt{2} \end{matrix} \right.\)
• At \(x=1\): \(y=1^{2}=1\) and \(y=\left| 2-1^{2} \right|=1\), so the two curves intersect at \(A(1,1)\).
• At \(x=\sqrt{2}\): \(y=x^{2}\) meets the horizontal line \(y=2\) at \(B\left( \sqrt{2},2 \right)\), while \(y=\left| 2-x^{2} \right|\) touches the x-axis at \(C\left( \sqrt{2},0 \right)\).
• For \(x \geq \sqrt{2}\): the branch \(y=x^{2}-2\) meets the line \(y=2\) at \(x^{2}-2=2 \Longrightarrow x=2\), giving \(D(2,2)\).
Step 2: Set Up the Definite Integrals Over \(\left[ 1,\sqrt{2} \right]\) and \(\left[ \sqrt{2},2 \right]\)
• On \(\left[ 1,\sqrt{2} \right]\), the upper boundary is \(y=x^{2}\) and the lower boundary is \(y=2-x^{2}\).
• On \(\left[ \sqrt{2},2 \right]\), the upper boundary is \(y=2\) and the lower boundary is \(y=x^{2}-2\).
Hence, the required area \(A\) is:
\[A=\int_{1}^{\sqrt{2}}\left[ x^{2}-\left( 2-x^{2} \right) \right] dx+\int_{\sqrt{2}}^{2}\left[ 2-\left( x^{2}-2 \right) \right] dx=\int_{1}^{\sqrt{2}}\left( 2x^{2}-2 \right)\ dx+\int_{\sqrt{2}}^{2}\left( 4-x^{2} \right)\ dx\]
Step 3: Evaluate the Integrals
\[I_{1}=\left[ \frac{2x^{3}}{3}-2x \right]_{1}^{\sqrt{2}}=\left( \frac{4\sqrt{2}}{3}-2\sqrt{2} \right)-\left( \frac{2}{3}-2 \right)=-\frac{2\sqrt{2}}{3}+\frac{4}{3}\]
\[I_{2}=\left[ 4x-\frac{x^{3}}{3} \right]_{\sqrt{2}}^{2}=\left( 8-\frac{8}{3} \right)-\left( 4\sqrt{2}-\frac{2\sqrt{2}}{3} \right)=\frac{16}{3}-\frac{10\sqrt{2}}{3}\]
Adding \(I_{1}\) and \(I_{2}\) together:
\[A=I_{1}+I_{2}=\left( \frac{4}{3}-\frac{2\sqrt{2}}{3} \right)+\left( \frac{16}{3}-\frac{10\sqrt{2}}{3} \right)=\frac{20-12\sqrt{2}}{3}\text{ sq. units}\]
Final Answer: The area of the bounded region is \(\frac{20-12\sqrt{2}}{3}\) square units.

IIT200200000Q10:
Step 1: Express the Volume \(V\) via Scalar Triple Product (Method 1 --- Geometric Inequality)
The volume \(V\) of the parallelopiped formed by \(\overrightarrow{a},\overrightarrow{b},\overrightarrow{c}\) is the magnitude of their scalar triple product:
\[V=\left| \overrightarrow{a} \cdot \left( \overrightarrow{b} \times \overrightarrow{c} \right) \right| \leq \left\| \overrightarrow{a} \right\|\ \left\| \overrightarrow{b} \right\|\ \left\| \overrightarrow{c} \right\|\]
Since \(a_{1},a_{2},a_{3} \geq 0\), all cross-terms \(2a_{i}a_{j} \geq 0\), so:
\[\left\| \overrightarrow{a} \right\|=\sqrt{a_{1}^{2}+a_{2}^{2}+a_{3}^{2}} \leq \sqrt{\left( a_{1}+a_{2}+a_{3} \right)^{2}}=a_{1}+a_{2}+a_{3}=\sum_{r=1}^{3}a_{r}\]
Similarly, for the non-negative components of \(\overrightarrow{b}\) and \(\overrightarrow{c}\):
\[\left\| \overrightarrow{b} \right\| \leq \sum_{r=1}^{3}b_{r}\quad \text{ and }\quad \left\| \overrightarrow{c} \right\| \leq \sum_{r=1}^{3}c_{r}\]
Therefore:
\[V \leq \left( \sum_{r=1}^{3}a_{r} \right)\left( \sum_{r=1}^{3}b_{r} \right)\left( \sum_{r=1}^{3}c_{r} \right)\]
Step 2: Alternative Verification via Determinant Expansion (Method 2 --- Algebraic Bound)
Expanding the determinant directly for \(a_{r},b_{r},c_{r} \geq 0\):
\(V=\left| \left| \begin{matrix} a_{1} & a_{2} & a_{3} \\ b_{1} & b_{2} & b_{3} \\ c_{1} & c_{2} & c_{3} \end{matrix} \right| \right| \leq \left( a_{1}+a_{2}+a_{3} \right)\left( b_{1}+b_{2}+b_{3} \right)\left( c_{1}+c_{2}+c_{3} \right)\)
because every positive and negative term in the determinant expansion is a subset of the \(27\) non-negative terms in the product \(\left( \sum a_{r} \right)\left( \sum b_{r} \right)\left( \sum c_{r} \right)\).
Step 3: Apply the AM--GM Inequality
Let \(S_{a}=\sum_{r=1}^{3}a_{r} \geq 0\), \(S_{b}=\sum_{r=1}^{3}b_{r} \geq 0\), and \(S_{c}=\sum_{r=1}^{3}c_{r} \geq 0\). By the AM--GM inequality:
\[\left( S_{a}S_{b}S_{c} \right)^{\frac{1}{3}} \leq \frac{S_{a}+S_{b}+S_{c}}{3}=\frac{\sum_{r=1}^{3}\left( a_{r}+b_{r}+c_{r} \right)}{3}=\frac{3L}{3}=L\]
Cubing both sides yields \(V \leq S_{a}S_{b}S_{c} \leq L^{3}\).
Conclusion: Therefore, \(V \leq L^{3}\). (Hence Proved)
IIT200200000Q11:
Step 1: Factor Out \(x\) and Absorb \(x=\left( x^{m} \right)^{\frac{1}{m}}\) into the Radical
Let \(I\) denote the given integral. Since \(x>0\), we factor \(x\) out of the first bracket:
\[x^{3m}+x^{2m}+x^{m}=\left( x^{3m-1}+x^{2m-1}+x^{m-1} \right) \cdot x\]
Since \(x>0\), we can write \(x=\left( x^{m} \right)^{\frac{1}{m}}\) and multiply it inside \(\left( 2x^{2m}+3x^{m}+6 \right)^{\frac{1}{m}}\):
\[x\left( 2x^{2m}+3x^{m}+6 \right)^{\frac{1}{m}}=\left( x^{m}\left( 2x^{2m}+3x^{m}+6 \right) \right)^{\frac{1}{m}}=\left( 2x^{3m}+3x^{2m}+6x^{m} \right)^{\frac{1}{m}}\]
Thus, the integral \(I\) becomes:
\[I=\int\left( x^{3m-1}+x^{2m-1}+x^{m-1} \right)\left( 2x^{3m}+3x^{2m}+6x^{m} \right)^{\frac{1}{m}}dx\]
Step 2: Perform the Substitution
Let \(t=2x^{3m}+3x^{2m}+6x^{m}\). Differentiating both sides with respect to \(x\):
\[dt=\left( 6mx^{3m-1}+6mx^{2m-1}+6mx^{m-1} \right)dx=6m\left( x^{3m-1}+x^{2m-1}+x^{m-1} \right)dx\]
\[\Longrightarrow \left( x^{3m-1}+x^{2m-1}+x^{m-1} \right)dx=\frac{dt}{6m}\]
Step 3: Integrate with Respect to \(t\) and Back-Substitute
\[I=\int t^{\frac{1}{m}}\frac{dt}{6m}=\frac{1}{6m} \cdot \frac{t^{\frac{1}{m}+1}}{\frac{1}{m}+1}+C=\frac{1}{6\left( m+1 \right)}t^{\frac{m+1}{m}}+C\]
Substituting back \(t=2x^{3m}+3x^{2m}+6x^{m}\):
\[I=\frac{1}{6\left( m+1 \right)}\left( 2x^{3m}+3x^{2m}+6x^{m} \right)^{\frac{m+1}{m}}+C\]
Final Answer: \(\int\left( x^{3m}+x^{2m}+x^{m} \right)\left( 2x^{2m}+3x^{m}+6 \right)^{\frac{1}{m}}dx=\frac{1}{6\left( m+1 \right)}\left( 2x^{3m}+3x^{2m}+6x^{m} \right)^{\frac{m+1}{m}}+C\).

IIT200200000Q12.t:
{{figure}}
Step 1: Determine the Composite Function \((g \circ f)(x)=g\left( f(x) \right)\)
From the definition of \(g\), we have:
\((g \circ f)(x)=g\left( f(x) \right)=\left\{ \begin{matrix} f(x)+1 & \text{if }f(x)<0 \\ \left( f(x)-1 \right)^{2}+b & \text{if }f(x) \geq 0 \end{matrix} \right.\)
Since \(a \geq 0\), we examine the sign of \(f(x)\) across the intervals of \(x\):
• For \(x<0\): \(f(x)=x+a\). Thus \(f(x)<0\) when \(x<-a\), and \(f(x) \geq 0\) when \(-a \leq x<0\).
• For \(x \geq 0\): \(f(x)=\left| x-1 \right| \geq 0\) for all \(x \geq 0\). Specifically, for \(0 \leq x<1\), \(f(x)=1-x\), so \(f(x)-1=-x\); and for \(x \geq 1\), \(f(x)=x-1\), so \(f(x)-1=x-2\).
Combining all branches, the explicit piecewise formula for \((g \circ f)(x)\) is:
\((g \circ f)(x)=\left\{ \begin{matrix} x+a+1 & \text{if }x<-a \\ \left( x+a-1 \right)^{2}+b & \text{if }-a \leq x<0 \\ x^{2}+b & \text{if }0 \leq x<1 \\ \left( x-2 \right)^{2}+b & \text{if }x \geq 1 \end{matrix} \right.\)
Step 2: Find \(a\) and \(b\) for Continuity of \((g \circ f)(x)\) on \(\mathbb{R}\)
• Continuity at \(x=-a\):
\[\lim\limits_{x \to -a^{-}}(g \circ f)(x)=\lim\limits_{x \to -a^{-}}\left( x+a+1 \right)=1\]
\[\lim\limits_{x \to -a^{+}}(g \circ f)(x)=\left( -a+a-1 \right)^{2}+b=1+b\]
For continuity at \(x=-a\), equate the two limits: \(1=1+b \Longrightarrow b=0\).
• Continuity at \(x=0\):
\[\lim\limits_{x \to 0^{-}}(g \circ f)(x)=\left( 0+a-1 \right)^{2}+b=\left( a-1 \right)^{2}+b,\quad \lim\limits_{x \to 0^{+}}(g \circ f)(x)=0^{2}+b=b\]
For continuity at \(x=0\), equate LHL and RHL: \(\left( a-1 \right)^{2}+b=b \Longrightarrow \left( a-1 \right)^{2}=0 \Longrightarrow a=1\).
(At \(x=1\), both branches give \(1+b=1\), so continuity holds everywhere.) Thus \(a=1\) and \(b=0\).
Step 3: Test Differentiability of \((g \circ f)(x)\) at \(x=0\) for \(a=1,b=0\)
Substituting \(a=1\) and \(b=0\) into the composite function gives:
\((g \circ f)(x)=\left\{ \begin{matrix} x+2 & \text{if }x<-1 \\ x^{2} & \text{if }-1 \leq x<1 \\ \left( x-2 \right)^{2} & \text{if }x \geq 1 \end{matrix} \right.\)
Computing the Left-Hand Derivative (LHD) and Right-Hand Derivative (RHD) at \(x=0\):
\[\text{LHD at }x=0:\quad \lim\limits_{h \to 0^{-}}\frac{(g \circ f)\left( 0+h \right)-(g \circ f)(0)}{h}=\lim\limits_{h \to 0^{-}}\frac{h^{2}-0}{h}=\lim\limits_{h \to 0^{-}}h=0\]
\[\text{RHD at }x=0:\quad \lim\limits_{h \to 0^{+}}\frac{(g \circ f)\left( 0+h \right)-(g \circ f)(0)}{h}=\lim\limits_{h \to 0^{+}}\frac{h^{2}-0}{h}=\lim\limits_{h \to 0^{+}}h=0\]
Since \(\text{LHD}=\text{RHD}=0\), the function \(g \circ f\) is differentiable at \(x=0\), and \((g \circ f)^{\prime}(0)=0\).
Final Answer: \(a=1\), \(b=0\); Yes, \((g \circ f)(x)\) is differentiable at \(x=0\) with derivative \((g \circ f)^{\prime}(0)=0\).

Method 1 (Geometrical / Section Formula Method):
Given that \(\alpha = \alpha_{1} + i\alpha_{2}\) and \(\beta = \beta_{1} + i\beta_{2}\), the relation is:
\[\left| \frac{z - \alpha}{z - \beta} \right| = k \Longrightarrow |z - \alpha| = k|z - \beta|\quad (k \neq 1)\]
{{figure}}
Let \(A(\alpha)\) and \(B(\beta)\) be the two fixed points in the Argand plane, and let \(R(z)\) be the moving point such that \(\frac{RA}{RB} = k\). The internal and external angle bisectors of \(\angle ARB\) meet the line joining \(A(\alpha)\) and \(B(\beta)\) at points \(P(z_{1})\) and \(Q(z_{2})\), dividing the segment \(AB\) internally and externally in the ratio \(k:1\), respectively:
\[z_{1} = \frac{k\beta + \alpha}{k + 1},\quad z_{2} = \frac{k\beta - \alpha}{k - 1}\]
Since the internal and external bisectors of an angle are perpendicular to each other, \(\angle PRQ = \frac{\pi}{2}\). Therefore, the locus of \(R(z)\) is a circle with \(PQ\) as its diameter.
• Centre of the circle (midpoint of \(PQ\)):
\[Centre = \frac{z_{1} + z_{2}}{2} = \frac{1}{2}\left( \frac{k\beta + \alpha}{k + 1} + \frac{k\beta - \alpha}{k - 1} \right) = \frac{\alpha - k^{2}\beta}{1 - k^{2}}\]
In component form, substituting \(\alpha = \alpha_{1} + i\alpha_{2}\) and \(\beta = \beta_{1} + i\beta_{2}\):
\[Centre = \left( \frac{\alpha_{1} - k^{2}\beta_{1}}{1 - k^{2}} \right) + i\left( \frac{\alpha_{2} - k^{2}\beta_{2}}{1 - k^{2}} \right)\]
• Radius of the circle (\(\frac{1}{2}|z_{1} - z_{2}|\)):
\[Radius = \frac{1}{2}\left| \frac{k\beta + \alpha}{k + 1} - \frac{k\beta - \alpha}{k - 1} \right| = \left| \frac{k(\alpha - \beta)}{1 - k^{2}} \right| = \frac{k\sqrt{(\alpha_{1} - \beta_{1})^{2} + (\alpha_{2} - \beta_{2})^{2}}}{|1 - k^{2}|}\]
Method 2 (Alternative Algebraic Method):
Squaring both sides of \(|z - \alpha| = k|z - \beta|\) and using \(|w|^{2} = w\overline{w}\):
\[(z - \alpha)\left(\overline{z} - \overline{\alpha}\right) = k^{2}(z - \beta)\left(\overline{z} - \overline{\beta}\right)\]
\[z\overline{z} - \alpha\overline{z} - \overline{\alpha}z + \alpha\overline{\alpha} = k^{2}\left( z\overline{z} - \beta\overline{z} - \overline{\beta}z + \beta\overline{\beta} \right)\]
Dividing throughout by \((1 - k^{2}) \neq 0\):
\[z\overline{z} - \left( \frac{\alpha - k^{2}\beta}{1 - k^{2}} \right)\overline{z} - \left( \frac{\overline{\alpha} - k^{2}\overline{\beta}}{1 - k^{2}} \right)z + \frac{\alpha\overline{\alpha} - k^{2}\beta\overline{\beta}}{1 - k^{2}} = 0\]
Comparing with the standard equation of a circle \(z\overline{z} + a\overline{z} + \overline{a}z + b = 0\), the centre and radius are:
\[Centre = \frac{\alpha - k^{2}\beta}{1 - k^{2}},\quad Radius = \sqrt{\frac{(\alpha - k^{2}\beta)\left(\overline{\alpha} - k^{2}\overline{\beta}\right)}{(1 - k^{2})^{2}} - \frac{\alpha\overline{\alpha} - k^{2}\beta\overline{\beta}}{1 - k^{2}}} = \left| \frac{k(\alpha - \beta)}{1 - k^{2}} \right|\]

IIT200400000Q02:
Given that \(\overrightarrow{a},\overrightarrow{b},\overrightarrow{c},\overrightarrow{d}\) are four distinct vectors satisfying:
\[\overrightarrow{a} \times \overrightarrow{b} = \overrightarrow{c} \times \overrightarrow{d}\quad \text{ and }\quad \overrightarrow{a} \times \overrightarrow{c} = \overrightarrow{b} \times \overrightarrow{d}\]
Subtracting the second equation from the first:
\[\overrightarrow{a} \times \left(\overrightarrow{b} - \overrightarrow{c}\right) = \left(\overrightarrow{c} - \overrightarrow{b}\right) \times \overrightarrow{d} = \overrightarrow{d} \times \left(\overrightarrow{b} - \overrightarrow{c}\right)\]
\[\left(\overrightarrow{a} - \overrightarrow{d}\right) \times \left(\overrightarrow{b} - \overrightarrow{c}\right) = \overrightarrow{0}\]
Since \(\overrightarrow{a},\overrightarrow{b},\overrightarrow{c},\overrightarrow{d}\) are distinct vectors, \(\overrightarrow{a} - \overrightarrow{d} \neq \overrightarrow{0}\) and \(\overrightarrow{b} - \overrightarrow{c} \neq \overrightarrow{0}\). Therefore, the non-zero vectors \(\left(\overrightarrow{a} - \overrightarrow{d}\right)\) and \(\left(\overrightarrow{b} - \overrightarrow{c}\right)\) are parallel:
\[\left(\overrightarrow{a} - \overrightarrow{d}\right) \parallel \left(\overrightarrow{b} - \overrightarrow{c}\right)\]
Because two non-zero parallel vectors cannot be perpendicular to each other, their dot product is non-zero:
\[\left(\overrightarrow{a} - \overrightarrow{d}\right) \cdot \left(\overrightarrow{b} - \overrightarrow{c}\right) \neq 0 \Longrightarrow \overrightarrow{a} \cdot \overrightarrow{b} - \overrightarrow{a} \cdot \overrightarrow{c} - \overrightarrow{d} \cdot \overrightarrow{b} + \overrightarrow{d} \cdot \overrightarrow{c} \neq 0\]
\[\Longrightarrow \overrightarrow{a} \cdot \overrightarrow{b} + \overrightarrow{c} \cdot \overrightarrow{d} \neq \overrightarrow{a} \cdot \overrightarrow{c} + \overrightarrow{b} \cdot \overrightarrow{d}\]
Hence proved.
IIT200400000Q03:
Consider \(n^{2}\) objects distributed in \(n\) groups, where each group contains \(n\) identical objects (i.e., \(n\) objects of the \(1^{st}\) kind, \(n\) objects of the \(2^{nd}\) kind, \(\ldots\), \(n\) objects of the \(n^{th}\) kind).
The total number of distinct arrangements (permutations) of these \(n^{2}\) objects taken all at a time is:
\[Number\ of\ arrangements = \frac{(n^{2})!}{underbrace{n!\ n!\ \ldots\ n!}_{n\ factors}} = \frac{(n^{2})!}{(n!)^{n}}\]
Since the number of arrangements of objects must be a positive integer, \(\frac{(n^{2})!}{(n!)^{n}}\) is an integer for every positive integer \(n\).
Hence proved.
IIT200400000Q04:
Method 1:
Using the given relation \(M^{T}M = I\):
\[(M - I)^{T} = M^{T} - I = M^{T} - M^{T}M = M^{T}(I - M)\]
Taking determinants on both sides and using \(\det(A^{T}) = \det(A)\), \(\det(AB) = \det(A)\det(B)\), and \(\det(I - M) = ( - 1)^{3}\det(M - I) = - \det(M - I)\) (since \(M\) is of order \(3 \times 3\)):
\[\det\left( (M - I)^{T} \right) = \det(M^{T})\det(I - M)\]
\[\det(M - I) = 1 \cdot \left( - \det(M - I) \right) \Longrightarrow 2\det(M - I) = 0 \Longrightarrow \det(M - I) = 0\]
Method 2 (Alternative):
\[\det(M - I) = \det(M - I)\det(M^{T}) = \det(MM^{T} - M^{T}) = \det(I - M^{T}) = - \det(M^{T} - I) = - \det\left( (M - I)^{T} \right) = - \det(M - I)\]
\[\Longrightarrow \det(M - I) = 0\]
Hence proved.
IIT200400000Q05:
Factoring \(\cos x\) out of the definite integral with respect to \(\theta\):
\[y(x) = \cos x\int_{\pi^{2}/16}^{x^{2}}{}\frac{\cos\sqrt{\theta}}{1 + \sin^{2}\sqrt{\theta}}\ d\theta\]
Differentiating with respect to \(x\) using the product rule and Leibniz's rule (for \(x > 0\)):
\[\frac{dy}{dx} = - \sin x\int_{\pi^{2}/16}^{x^{2}}{}\frac{\cos\sqrt{\theta}}{1 + \sin^{2}\sqrt{\theta}}\ d\theta + \frac{2x\cos x \cdot \cos x}{1 + \sin^{2}x}\]
Evaluating at \(x = \pi\) (where \(\sin\pi = 0\) and \(\cos\pi = - 1\)):
\[\left. \ \frac{dy}{dx} \right|_{x = \pi} = 0 + \frac{2\pi( - 1)( - 1)}{1 + 0} = 2\pi\]
IIT200400000Q06:
Let the equation of the base plane \(ABCD\) be \(ax + by + cz + d = 0\), the coordinates of \(A''\) be \((\alpha,\beta,\gamma)\), and the initial perpendicular height of the parallelepiped \(T\) above face \(ABCD\) be \(h\).
Since the base face \(ABCD\) remains unchanged and the volume of \(S\) is reduced to \(90\%\) of the volume of \(T\), the new height of \(S\) (the perpendicular distance of \(A''(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)\) from plane \(ABCD\)) is \(0.9h\):
\[\frac{|a\alpha + b\beta + c\gamma + d|}{\sqrt{a^{2} + b^{2} + c^{2}}} = 0.9h \Longrightarrow a\alpha + b\beta + c\gamma + d = \pm 0.9h\sqrt{a^{2} + b^{2} + c^{2}}\]
Replacing \((\alpha,\beta,\gamma)\) with \((x,y,z)\), the locus of \(A''\) is \(ax + by + cz + d = \pm 0.9h\sqrt{a^{2} + b^{2} + c^{2}}\), which represents a plane parallel to the plane \(ABCD\).
Hence proved.
IIT200400000Q07:
Rewriting the given limit:
\[\lim\limits_{n \to \infty}\left[ \frac{2}{\pi}(n + 1)\cos^{- 1}\left( \frac{1}{n} \right) - n \right] = \lim\limits_{n \to \infty}n\left[ \frac{2}{\pi}\left( 1 + \frac{1}{n} \right)\cos^{- 1}\left( \frac{1}{n} \right) - 1 \right] = \lim\limits_{n \to \infty}nf\left( \frac{1}{n} \right) = f'(0)\]
where \(f(x) = \frac{2}{\pi}(1 + x)\cos^{- 1}x - 1\). Clearly, \(f(0) = \frac{2}{\pi}(1)\left( \frac{\pi}{2} \right) - 1 = 0\).
Differentiating \(f(x)\) with respect to \(x\):
\[f'(x) = \frac{2}{\pi}\left[ (1 + x)\frac{- 1}{\sqrt{1 - x^{2}}} + \cos^{- 1}x \right]\]
Evaluating at \(x = 0\):
\[f'(0) = \frac{2}{\pi}\left[ - 1 + \frac{\pi}{2} \right] = \frac{2}{\pi}\left[ \frac{\pi - 2}{2} \right] = 1 - \frac{2}{\pi}\]
IIT200400000Q09:
Let \((l,m,n)\) be the direction ratios of the normal to the required plane. Since the plane is parallel to the lines with direction ratios \((1,0, - 1)\) and \(( - 1,1,0)\):
\[l - n = 0\quad \text{ and }\quad - l + m = 0 \Longrightarrow l = m = n\]
Hence, the equation of the plane passing through \((1,1,1)\) is:
\[(x - 1) + (y - 1) + (z - 1) = 0 \Longrightarrow x + y + z = 3 \Longrightarrow \frac{x}{3} + \frac{y}{3} + \frac{z}{3} = 1\]
Its intercepts with the coordinate axes are \(A(3,0,0)\), \(B(0,3,0)\), and \(C(0,0,3)\). Therefore, the volume of the tetrahedron \(OABC\) is:
\[V = \frac{1}{6}\left| \begin{matrix} 3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3 \end{matrix} \right| = \frac{27}{6} = \frac{9}{2}\ cubic\ \text{units}\]
IIT200400000Q10:
Since \(A\) and \(B\) are independent events, \(P(A' \cap B') = P(A')P(B')\), and \(P(A \cup B) \leq P(A) + P(B)\). Thus:
\[P(A \cup B) \cdot P(A' \cap B') \leq \left( P(A) + P(B) \right)P(A')P(B')\]
\[= P(A)P(A')P(B') + P(B)P(A')P(B')\]
\[= P(A)P(B')\left( 1 - P(A) \right) + P(B)P(A')\left( 1 - P(B) \right)\]
Since \(1 - P(A) \leq 1\) and \(1 - P(B) \leq 1\):
\[P(A \cup B) \cdot P(A' \cap B') \leq P(A)P(B') + P(B)P(A') = P(C)\]
Hence proved.

IIT200400000Q11.t:
Given the differential equation of the curve:
\[\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{(x + 1)^{2} + y - 3}{x + 1} = (x + 1) + \frac{y - 3}{x + 1}\]
{{figure}}
Putting \(X = x + 1\) and \(Y = y - 3\), we have \(\frac{dY}{dX} = \frac{dy}{dx}\):
\[\frac{dY}{dX} - \frac{Y}{X} = X\]
This is a linear differential equation with integrating factor \(I.F. = e^{- \int_{}^{}\frac{1}{X}\ dX} = \frac{1}{X}\):
\[\frac{1}{X} \cdot Y = X + c \Longrightarrow \frac{y - 3}{x + 1} = (x + 1) + c\]
Since the curve passes through \((2,0)\):
\[\frac{0 - 3}{2 + 1} = (2 + 1) + c \Longrightarrow - 1 = 3 + c \Longrightarrow c = - 4\]
Thus, the equation of the curve is:
\[y - 3 = (x + 1)^{2} - 4(x + 1) \Longrightarrow y = x^{2} - 2x\]
The required area enclosed by \(y = x^{2} - 2x\) and the x-axis in the fourth quadrant (from \(x = 0\) to \(x = 2\)) is:
\[Required\ \text{Area} = \left| \int_{0}^{2}{}(x^{2} - 2x)\ dx \right| = \left| \left[ \frac{x^{3}}{3} - x^{2} \right]_{0}^{2} \right| = \left| \frac{8}{3} - 4 \right| = \frac{4}{3}\text{ sq. units}\]

IIT200400000Q12:
The equation of any circle touching the line \(2x + 3y + 1 = 0\) at \((1, - 1)\) is:
\[(x - 1)^{2} + (y + 1)^{2} + \lambda(2x + 3y + 1) = 0\]
\[x^{2} + y^{2} + (2\lambda - 2)x + (3\lambda + 2)y + (\lambda + 2) = 0\]
This circle is orthogonal to the circle having \((0, - 1)\) and \(( - 2,3)\) as endpoints of a diameter:
\[(x - 0)(x + 2) + (y + 1)(y - 3) = 0 \Longrightarrow x^{2} + y^{2} + 2x - 2y - 3 = 0\]
Applying the condition of orthogonality \(2g_{1}g_{2} + 2f_{1}f_{2} = c_{1} + c_{2}\):
\[2\left( \frac{2\lambda - 2}{2} \right)\left( \frac{2}{2} \right) + 2\left( \frac{3\lambda + 2}{2} \right)\left( \frac{- 2}{2} \right) = (\lambda + 2) - 3\]
\[(2\lambda - 2) - (3\lambda + 2) = \lambda - 1 \Longrightarrow - \lambda - 4 = \lambda - 1 \Longrightarrow \lambda = - \frac{3}{2}\]
Substituting \(\lambda = - \frac{3}{2}\) gives the required circle:
\[2x^{2} + 2y^{2} - 10x - 5y + 1 = 0\]
IIT200400000Q13:
Writing the parabola in standard form:
\[(y - 1)^{2} = 4(x - 1)\]
Any point on the parabola is \(P\left( 1 + t^{2},1 + 2t \right)\). The equation of the tangent at \(P\) is:
\[t(y - 1) = x - 1 + t^{2}\]
which meets the directrix \(x = 0\) at \(Q\left( 0,1 + t - \frac{1}{t} \right)\).
Let \(R\) be \((h,k)\). Since \(R\) divides \(QP\) externally in the ratio \(\frac{1}{2}:1\), \(Q\) is the midpoint of \(RP\):
\[0 = \frac{h + 1 + t^{2}}{2} \Longrightarrow t^{2} = - (h + 1)\]
\[1 + t - \frac{1}{t} = \frac{k + 1 + 2t}{2} \Longrightarrow 2 + 2t - \frac{2}{t} = k + 1 + 2t \Longrightarrow t = \frac{2}{1 - k}\]
Eliminating \(t\):
\[\frac{4}{(1 - k)^{2}} + (h + 1) = 0 \Longrightarrow (k - 1)^{2}(h + 1) + 4 = 0\]
Replacing \((h,k)\) with \((x,y)\), the locus of \(R\) is:
\[(y - 1)^{2}(x + 1) + 4 = 0\]
IIT200400000Q14:
Let \(I = \int_{- \pi/3}^{\pi/3}{}\frac{\pi + 4x^{3}}{2 - \cos\left( |x| + \frac{\pi}{3} \right)}\ dx\). Using \(\int_{- a}^{a}{}f(x)\ dx = \int_{0}^{a}{}[ f(x) + f( - x)]\ dx\):
\[2I = \int_{- \pi/3}^{\pi/3}{}\frac{2\pi\ dx}{2 - \cos\left( |x| + \frac{\pi}{3} \right)} \Longrightarrow I = \int_{0}^{\pi/3}{}\frac{2\pi\ dx}{2 - \cos\left( x + \frac{\pi}{3} \right)}\]
Substitute \(t = x + \frac{\pi}{3}\):
\[I = \int_{\pi/3}^{2\pi/3}{}\frac{2\pi\ dt}{2 - \cos t} = 2\pi\int_{\pi/3}^{2\pi/3}{}\frac{\sec^{2}\frac{t}{2}\ dt}{1 + 3\tan^{2}\frac{t}{2}}\]
Put \(u = \tan\frac{t}{2} \Longrightarrow du = \frac{1}{2}\sec^{2}\frac{t}{2}\ dt\):
\[I = 2\pi\int_{1/\sqrt{3}}^{\sqrt{3}}{}\frac{2\ du}{1 + 3u^{2}} = \frac{4\pi}{\sqrt{3}}\left[ \tan^{- 1}\left(\sqrt{3}u\right) \right]_{1/\sqrt{3}}^{\sqrt{3}} = \frac{4\pi}{\sqrt{3}}\left[ \tan^{- 1}3 - \frac{\pi}{4} \right] = \frac{4\pi}{\sqrt{3}}\tan^{- 1}\left( \frac{1}{2} \right)\]
IIT200400000Q15:
Expanding the product:
\[(1 + a)(1 + b)(1 + c) = 1 + a + b + c + ab + bc + ca + abc\]
Applying \(AM \geq GM\) to the \(7\) positive terms \(a,b,c,ab,bc,ca,abc\):
\[\frac{(1 + a)(1 + b)(1 + c) - 1}{7} = \frac{a + b + c + ab + bc + ca + abc}{7} \geq (a \cdot b \cdot c \cdot ab \cdot bc \cdot ca \cdot abc)^{1/7} = \left( a^{4}b^{4}c^{4} \right)^{1/7}\]
\[\Longrightarrow (1 + a)(1 + b)(1 + c) - 1 \geq 7\left( a^{4}b^{4}c^{4} \right)^{1/7} \Longrightarrow (1 + a)(1 + b)(1 + c) > 7\left( a^{4}b^{4}c^{4} \right)^{1/7}\]
Raising both positive sides to the \(7^{th}\) power:
\[[(1 + a)(1 + b)(1 + c)]^{7} > 7^{7}a^{4}b^{4}c^{4}\]
Hence proved.
IIT200400000Q16:
Since \(f(x)\) is differentiable at \(x = 0\), it is continuous at \(x = 0\), so \(f(0^{+}) = f(0^{-}) = f(0) = \frac{1}{2}\):
\[f(0^{+}) = \lim\limits_{x \to 0^{+}}\frac{e^{ax/2} - 1}{x} = \lim\limits_{x \to 0^{+}}\frac{e^{ax/2} - 1}{ax/2} \cdot \frac{a}{2} = \frac{a}{2}\]
\[b\sin^{- 1}\left( \frac{c}{2} \right) = \frac{a}{2} = \frac{1}{2} \Longrightarrow a = 1\]
Now equating the left-hand and right-hand derivatives at \(x = 0\):
\[Lf'(0) = \lim\limits_{h \to 0^{-}}\frac{b\sin^{- 1}\left( \frac{h + c}{2} \right) - \frac{1}{2}}{h} = \frac{b/2}{\sqrt{1 - \frac{c^{2}}{4}}} = \frac{b}{\sqrt{4 - c^{2}}}\]
\[Rf'(0) = \lim\limits_{h \to 0^{+}}\frac{\frac{e^{h/2} - 1}{h} - \frac{1}{2}}{h} = \frac{1}{8}\]
Since \(Lf'(0) = Rf'(0)\):
\[\frac{b}{\sqrt{4 - c^{2}}} = \frac{1}{8} \Longrightarrow 64b^{2} = 4 - c^{2}\]

IIT200400000Q17.t:
Let \(f(x) = 3x^{2} + (3 - 2\pi)x - \pi\sin x\). Then:
\[f(0) = 0,\quad f\left( \frac{\pi}{2} \right) = \frac{3\pi^{2}}{4} + \frac{3\pi}{2} - \pi^{2} - \pi = \frac{\pi(2 - \pi)}{4} < 0\]
{{figure}}
Differentiating \(f(x)\) twice:
\[f'(x) = 6x + 3 - 2\pi - \pi\cos x,\quad f''(x) = 6 + \pi\sin x > 0\quad \forall x \in \left[ 0,\frac{\pi}{2} \right]\]
Since \(f''(x) > 0\), \(f'(x)\) is strictly increasing on \(\left[ 0,\frac{\pi}{2} \right]\), so \(f(x)\) has no local maximum in \(\left[ 0,\frac{\pi}{2} \right]\). Since \(f(0) = 0\) and \(f\left( \frac{\pi}{2} \right) < 0\), the graph of \(f(x)\) lies on or below the x-axis throughout \(\left[ 0,\frac{\pi}{2} \right]\):
\[f(x) \leq 0\quad \forall x \in \left[ 0,\frac{\pi}{2} \right] \Longrightarrow 3x^{2} + 3x \leq 2\pi x + \pi\sin x \Longrightarrow \sin x + 2x \geq \frac{3x(x + 1)}{\pi}\]
Hence proved.

IIT200400000Q18:
Since \(AX = U\) has infinitely many solutions, \(|A| = |A_{1}| = |A_{2}| = |A_{3}| = 0\):
\[|A| = \left| \begin{matrix} a & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & c & b \\ 1 & d & b \end{matrix} \right| = (ab - 1)(c - d) = 0\]
\[|A_{1}| = \left| \begin{matrix} a & 0 & f \\ 1 & c & g \\ 1 & d & h \end{matrix} \right| = 0,\quad |A_{2}| = \left| \begin{matrix} a & f & 1 \\ 1 & g & b \\ 1 & h & b \end{matrix} \right| = 0,\quad |A_{3}| = \left| \begin{matrix} f & 0 & 1 \\ g & c & b \\ h & d & b \end{matrix} \right| = 0\]
Since the second and third rows of \([ A|U]\) represent parallel planes \(x + cy + bz = g\) and \(x + dy + bz = h\), infinitely many solutions require \(c = d\) and \(g = h\).
Now for the system \(BX = V\):
\[|B| = \left| \begin{matrix} a & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & d & c \\ f & g & h \end{matrix} \right| = 0\quad (since\ C_{2}\ \text{ and }\ C_{3}\ are\ identical\ as\ c = d,g = h)\]
Thus \(BX = V\) cannot have a unique solution. Moreover:
\[|B_{1}| = \left| \begin{matrix} a^{2} & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & d & c \\ 0 & g & h \end{matrix} \right| = 0,\quad |B_{2}| = \left| \begin{matrix} a & a^{2} & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & c \\ f & 0 & h \end{matrix} \right| = a^{2}cf = a^{2}df,\quad |B_{3}| = \left| \begin{matrix} a & 1 & a^{2} \\ 0 & d & 0 \\ f & g & 0 \end{matrix} \right| = - a^{2}df\]
If \(afd \neq 0\), then \(|B_{2}| \neq 0\) and \(|B_{3}| \neq 0\) while \(|B| = 0\), so \(BX = V\) has no solution.
Hence proved.
IIT200400000Q20:
Since \(P_{1}\) and \(P_{2}\) pass through the origin \(O\) and are distinct, their intersection \(P_{1} \cap P_{2}\) is a line through \(O\) distinct from both \(L_{1}\) and \(L_{2}\). Choose three non-origin points \(A,B,C\) as follows:
1. \(A\) lies on \(L_{1}\) (since \(L_{1} \subset P_{1}\) and \(L_{1}not \subset P_{2}\), \(A\) does not lie on \(P_{2}\)).
2. \(B\) lies on the line of intersection of \(P_{1}\) and \(P_{2}\) (so \(B\) lies on \(P_{1}\) not on \(L_{1}\), and also lies on \(P_{2}\) not on \(L_{2}\)).
3. \(C\) lies on \(L_{2}\) on the plane \(P_{2}\) (since \(L_{2} \subset P_{2}\) and \(L_{2}not \subset P_{1}\), \(C\) does not lie on \(P_{1}\)).
Now taking the permutation \([ A',B',C'] = [ C,B,A]\) of \([ A,B,C]\):
• \(A' = C\) lies on \(L_{2}\),
• \(B' = B\) lies on \(P_{2}\) not on \(L_{2}\),
• \(C' = A\) lies on \(L_{1}\) and does not lie on \(P_{2}\).
Hence, the permutation \([ A',B',C'] = [ C,B,A]\) satisfies both (i) and (ii).

A vector in the plane of \(\overrightarrow{a}\) and \(\overrightarrow{b}\) is \(\overrightarrow{a} + \lambda\overrightarrow{b} = (1 + \lambda)\hat{i} + (2 - \lambda)\hat{j} + (1 + \lambda)\hat{k}\). Its projection on \(\overrightarrow{c}\) is \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\):

IIT200700001Q45:
Using the sum and product of roots for the two quadratic equations:
\[\alpha + \beta = p,\quad \frac{\alpha}{2} + 2\beta = q,\quad \text{ and }\quad \alpha\beta = \left( \frac{\alpha}{2} \right)(2\beta) = r.\]
Subtracting \(\frac{1}{2}(\alpha + \beta) = \frac{p}{2}\) from \(\frac{\alpha}{2} + 2\beta = q\) gives:
\[\frac{3}{2}\beta = q - \frac{p}{2} = \frac{2q - p}{2} \Longrightarrow \beta = \frac{2q - p}{3}.\]
Substituting \(\beta\) into \(\alpha = p - \beta\) gives \(\alpha = p - \frac{2q - p}{3} = \frac{2(2p - q)}{3}\).
Therefore, \(r = \alpha\beta = \left( \frac{2(2p - q)}{3} \right)\left( \frac{2q - p}{3} \right) = \frac{2}{9}(2p - q)(2q - p)\).
IIT200700001Q46:
Rewrite the given limit by adding and subtracting \(x^{2}f(x)\) in the numerator:
\[\lim\limits_{t \to x}\ \frac{\left( t^{2} - x^{2} \right)f(x) - x^{2}\left( f(t) - f(x) \right)}{t - x} = 2xf(x) - x^{2}f^{\prime}(x) = 1.\]
Divide both sides by \(- x^{4}\) (for \(x > 0\)):
\[\frac{x^{2}f^{\prime}(x) - 2xf(x)}{x^{4}} = - \frac{1}{x^{4}} \Longrightarrow \frac{d}{dx}\left( \frac{f(x)}{x^{2}} \right) = - \frac{1}{x^{4}}.\]
Integrating with respect to \(x\) yields \(\frac{f(x)}{x^{2}} = \frac{1}{3x^{3}} + C \Longrightarrow f(x) = \frac{1}{3x} + Cx^{2}\).
Using \(f(1) = 1\) gives \(1 = \frac{1}{3} + C \Longrightarrow C = \frac{2}{3}\). Thus, \(f(x) = \frac{1}{3x} + \frac{2x^{2}}{3}\).
IIT200700001Q47:
Let \(B\) be the event that each of the \(4\) American men is seated adjacent to his wife, and let \(A\) be the event that the Indian man is seated adjacent to his wife.
• Count for \(B\): Treat each of the \(4\) American couples as a single block (\(4\) blocks, each internally permutable in \(2!\) ways) along with the Indian man and his wife (\(2\) individuals). This gives \(4 + 2 = 6\) objects around a circular table: \(n(B) = (6 - 1)! \cdot (2!)^{4} = 5! \cdot 2^{4}\).
• Count for \(A \cap B\): Treat all \(5\) couples as \(5\) blocks around the circular table: \(n(A \cap B) = (5 - 1)! \cdot (2!)^{5} = 4! \cdot 2^{5}\).
Hence, the required conditional probability is \(P(A \mid B) = \frac{n(A \cap B)}{n(B)} = \frac{4! \cdot 2^{5}}{5! \cdot 2^{4}} = \frac{2}{5}\).
IIT200700001Q48:
The equation of the tangent to \(y = e^{x}\) at \(\left( c,e^{c} \right)\) is:
\[y = e^{c} + e^{c}(x - c) = e^{c}(1 + x - c).\]
The equation of the secant line joining \(\left( c - 1,e^{c - 1} \right)\) and \(\left( c + 1,e^{c + 1} \right)\) is:
\[y - e^{c - 1} = \frac{e^{c + 1} - e^{c - 1}}{(c + 1) - (c - 1)}(x - c + 1) \Longrightarrow y = e^{c}\left[ e^{- 1} + \frac{e - e^{- 1}}{2}(x - c + 1) \right].\]
At the point of intersection, equating the two expressions for \(y\) and dividing by \(e^{c} > 0\) gives:
\[1 + (x - c) = \frac{e + e^{- 1}}{2} + \left( \frac{e - e^{- 1}}{2} \right)(x - c) \Longrightarrow (x - c)\left( \frac{e - e^{- 1} - 2}{2} \right) = 1 - \frac{e + e^{- 1}}{2} < 0.\]
Since \(e \approx 2.718\), we have \(e - e^{- 1} > 2.718 - 0.368 = 2.35 > 2\) and \(\frac{e + e^{- 1}}{2} > 1\). Therefore \(x - c < 0 \Longrightarrow x < c\), so the intersection lies on the left of \(x = c\).

As \(x \to \frac{\pi}{4}\), \(\sec^{2}x \to 2\), so the limit is of the indeterminate form \(\frac{0}{0}\).

\[L = \lim\limits_{x \to \frac{\pi}{4}}\ \frac{f\left( \sec^{2}x \right) \cdot \frac{d}{dx}\left( \sec^{2}x \right)}{2x} = \lim\limits_{x \to \frac{\pi}{4}}\ \frac{f\left( \sec^{2}x \right) \cdot 2\sec^{2}xtan\ x}{2x}.\]

Write the ellipse \(3x^{2} + 4y^{2} = 12\) in standard form: \(\frac{x^{2}}{4} + \frac{y^{2}}{3} = 1\).
Here \(A^{2} = 4\) and \(B^{2} = 3\), so its foci are at \(\left( \pm \sqrt{A^{2} - B^{2}},0 \right) = ( \pm 1,0)\).
Let the confocal hyperbola be \(\frac{x^{2}}{a^{2}} - \frac{y^{2}}{b^{2}} = 1\). Since its transverse axis has length \(2a = 2sin\ \theta\), we have \(a = sin\ \theta\).

Hence the equation of the hyperbola is \(\frac{x^{2}}{\sin^{2}\theta} - \frac{y^{2}}{\cos^{2}\theta} = 1 \Longrightarrow x^{2}{cosec\ }^{2}\theta - y^{2}\sec^{2}\theta = 1\).
IIT200700001Q51:
The three given vectors are coplanar if and only if their scalar triple product vanishes:

Adding \(C_{2}\) and \(C_{3}\) to \(C_{1}\) gives \(\left( 2 - \lambda^{2} \right)\) in each entry of the first column, and subtracting \(R_{1}\) from \(R_{2}\) and \(R_{3}\) yields:
\[\left( 2 - \lambda^{2} \right)\left( 1 + \lambda^{2} \right)^{2} = 0.\]
For real \(\lambda\), \(1 + \lambda^{2} \neq 0\), so \(\lambda^{2} = 2 \Longrightarrow \lambda = \pm \sqrt{2}\). Thus there are two distinct real values of \(\lambda\).

Take East along the positive real axis and North along the positive imaginary axis.
The first displacement of \(3\) units towards north-east (\(\text{N }45^{{^\circ}}\text{ E}\)) makes an angle of \(\frac{\pi}{4}\) with the positive real axis, so \(z_{1} = 3e^{i\pi/4}\).
The second displacement of \(4\) units towards north-west (\(\text{N }45^{{^\circ}}\text{ W}\)) makes an angle of \(\frac{3\pi}{4} = \frac{\pi}{4} + \frac{\pi}{2}\) with the positive real axis, so it equals \(4e^{i3\pi/4} = 4ie^{i\pi/4}\).

Since \(H_{1},H_{2},\ldots,H_{n}\) are mutually exclusive and exhaustive events, \(\sum_{i = 1}^{n}P\left( H_{i} \right) = P(S) = 1\), so STATEMENT-2 is True.
By conditional probability, \(P\left( H_{i} \mid E \right) = \frac{P\left( H_{i} \cap E \right)}{P(E)} = \frac{P\left( E \mid H_{i} \right)P\left( H_{i} \right)}{P(E)}\).

In the regular hexagon \(PQRSTU\), \(\overrightarrow{RS} + \overrightarrow{ST} = \overrightarrow{RT}\). Since \(\sin(x + \pi) = - sin\ x\), squaring gives \(\sin^{2}(x + \pi) = \sin^{2}x\) for all real \(x\) (STATEMENT-2 is True).
Evaluating the indefinite integral \(F(x) = \int\sin^{2}x\ dx = \int\frac{1 - cos\ 2x}{2}\ dx = \frac{x}{2} - \frac{sin\ 2x}{4} + C\):
\[F(x + \pi) = \frac{x + \pi}{2} - \frac{\sin(2x + 2\pi)}{4} + C = F(x) + \frac{\pi}{2} \neq F(x).\]

IIT200700001Q58:
The A.P. has first term \(a = r\) and common difference \(d = 2r - 1\). The sum of its first \(r\) terms is:
\[V_{r} = \frac{r}{2}\left[ 2r + (r - 1)(2r - 1) \right] = \frac{r}{2}\left( 2r^{2} - r + 1 \right) = r^{3} - \frac{1}{2}r^{2} + \frac{1}{2}r.\]
Summing \(V_{r}\) from \(r = 1\) to \(n\) using standard power sums:
\[\sum_{r = 1}^{n}V_{r} = \left[ \frac{n(n + 1)}{2} \right]^{2} - \frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{n(n + 1)(2n + 1)}{6} + \frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{n(n + 1)}{2}\]
\[\sum_{r = 1}^{n}V_{r} = \frac{n(n + 1)}{12}\left[ 3n(n + 1) - (2n + 1) + 3 \right] = \frac{1}{12}n(n + 1)\left( 3n^{2} + n + 2 \right).\]
IIT200700001Q59:
Using \(V_{r} = r^{3} - \frac{1}{2}r^{2} + \frac{1}{2}r\), compute \(T_{r} = V_{r + 1} - V_{r} - 2\):
\[V_{r + 1} - V_{r} = \left[ (r + 1)^{3} - r^{3} \right] - \frac{1}{2}\left[ (r + 1)^{2} - r^{2} \right] + \frac{1}{2}\left[ (r + 1) - r \right] = \left( 3r^{2} + 3r + 1 \right) - \left( r + \frac{1}{2} \right) + \frac{1}{2} = 3r^{2} + 2r + 1.\]
Therefore, \(T_{r} = \left( 3r^{2} + 2r + 1 \right) - 2 = 3r^{2} + 2r - 1 = (r + 1)(3r - 1)\).
For every integer \(r \geq 1\), both factors \((r + 1) \geq 2\) and \((3r - 1) \geq 2\) are integers greater than \(1\), so \(T_{r}\) is always a composite number.
IIT200700001Q60:
From Solution 59, \(T_{r} = 3r^{2} + 2r - 1\). Therefore:
\[Q_{r} = T_{r + 1} - T_{r} = \left[ 3(r + 1)^{2} + 2(r + 1) - 1 \right] - \left( 3r^{2} + 2r - 1 \right) = 3(2r + 1) + 2 = 6r + 5.\]
Since \(Q_{r + 1} - Q_{r} = 6(r + 1) + 5 - (6r + 5) = 6\) is constant for all \(r \geq 1\), the sequence \(Q_{1},Q_{2},Q_{3},\ldots\) is an A.P. with common difference \(6\).

Substitute \(y^{2} = 8x\) into \(x^{2} + y^{2} = 9\): \(x^{2} + 8x - 9 = 0 \Longrightarrow (x + 9)(x - 1) = 0\). Since \(y^{2} = 8x \geq 0\), we have \(x = 1\) and \(y = \pm 2\sqrt{2}\).

In \(\triangle PRS\), the vertices are \(P\left( 1,2\sqrt{2} \right)\), \(R(9,0)\), and \(S( - 1,0)\).

The determinant of the coefficient matrix of the homogeneous system is:
\(\Delta = \left| \begin{matrix} a & b & c \\ b & c & a \\ c & a & b \end{matrix} \right| = - \left( a^{3} + b^{3} + c^{3} - 3abc \right) = - (a + b + c)\left( a^{2} + b^{2} + c^{2} - ab - bc - ca \right).\)
Note that for real \(a,b,c\), \(a^{2} + b^{2} + c^{2} - ab - bc - ca = \frac{1}{2}\left[ (a - b)^{2} + (b - c)^{2} + (c - a)^{2} \right] = 0 \Longleftrightarrow a = b = c\).
• (A): \(a + b + c \neq 0\) and \(a = b = c \Longrightarrow a = b = c \neq 0\). All three equations reduce to \(x + y + z = 0\), representing identical planes (r).
• (B): \(a + b + c = 0\) and not all of \(a,b,c\) are equal. Then \(\Delta = 0\), and \((x,y,z) = (t,t,t)\) satisfies all three equations, while the planes are non-parallel, so their intersection is the line \(x = y = z\) (q).
• (C): \(a + b + c \neq 0\) and \(a^{2} + b^{2} + c^{2} \neq ab + bc + ca \Longrightarrow \Delta \neq 0\). The homogeneous system has only the trivial solution \((0,0,0)\), so the planes meet only at a single point (p).
• (D): \(a + b + c = 0\) and \(a = b = c \Longrightarrow a = b = c = 0\). Every \((x,y,z) \in {\mathbb{R}}^{3}\) satisfies \(0x + 0y + 0z = 0\), representing the whole of three-dimensional space (s).

Analyze each function on the open interval \(( - 1,1)\):
• (A) \(f(x) = x|x| = \begin{cases} -x^2, & -1 < x < 0 \\ x^2, & 0 \le x < 1 \end{cases}\): Continuous on \(( - 1,1)\), differentiable everywhere on \(( - 1,1)\) with \(f^{\prime}(x) = 2|x| \geq 0\) (and \(f^{\prime}(0) = 0\)), and strictly increasing on \(( - 1,1)\). Thus (A) → (p), (q), (r).
• (B) \(f(x) = \sqrt{|x|}\): Continuous on \(( - 1,1)\) (p), not differentiable at \(x = 0 \in ( - 1,1)\) (s), and decreases on \(( - 1,0)\) then increases on \((0,1)\). Thus (B) → (p), (s).
• (C) \(f(x) = x + [x] = \begin{cases} x - 1, & -1 < x < 0 \\ x, & 0 \le x < 1 \end{cases}\): Discontinuous (and hence not differentiable) at \(x = 0 \in ( - 1,1)\) (s), and strictly increasing on \(( - 1,1)\) (r). Thus (C) → (r), (s).
• (D) \(f(x) = |x - 1| + |x + 1| = (1 - x) + (x + 1) = 2\) for all \(x \in (-1, 1)\): Constant on \(( - 1,1)\), hence continuous (p) and differentiable (q) on \(( - 1,1)\), but not strictly increasing. Thus (D) → (p), (q).

Since \(|z| = 1\), we have \(z\overline{z} = 1 \Longrightarrow \frac{1}{z} = \overline{z}\).
Let \(z = cos\ \theta + isin\ \theta\) with \(\theta \neq k\pi\) (since \(z \neq \pm 1\)). Then:
\[w = \frac{z}{1 - z^{2}} = \frac{1}{z^{- 1} - z} = \frac{1}{\overline{z} - z} = \frac{1}{- 2isin\ \theta} = \frac{i}{2sin\ \theta}.\]
Since \(Re\ (w) = 0\) for all \(z\) with \(|z| = 1,z \neq \pm 1\), all values of \(\frac{z}{1 - z^{2}}\) are purely imaginary and lie on the \(y\)-axis.
IIT200700002Q47:
Using De Morgan's Law and inclusion-exclusion inside the event \(G\):
\[P\left( E^{c} \cap F^{c} \mid G \right) = \frac{P\left( (E \cup F)^{c} \cap G \right)}{P(G)} = \frac{P(G) - P\left( (E \cup F) \cap G \right)}{P(G)}\]
\[P\left( E^{c} \cap F^{c} \mid G \right) = \frac{P(G) - P(E \cap G) - P(F \cap G) + P(E \cap F \cap G)}{P(G)}.\]
Since \(E,F,G\) are pairwise independent, \(P(E \cap G) = P(E)P(G)\) and \(P(F \cap G) = P(F)P(G)\), and we are given \(P(E \cap F \cap G) = 0\):
\[P\left( E^{c} \cap F^{c} \mid G \right) = \frac{P(G) - P(E)P(G) - P(F)P(G) + 0}{P(G)} = 1 - P(E) - P(F) = P\left( E^{c} \right) - P(F).\]
IIT200700002Q48:
By the inverse function derivative rule, \(\frac{dx}{dy} = \left( \frac{dy}{dx} \right)^{- 1}\).
Differentiating with respect to \(y\) using the chain rule:
\[\frac{d^{2}x}{dy^{2}} = \frac{d}{dy}\left[ \left( \frac{dy}{dx} \right)^{- 1} \right] = \frac{d}{dx}\left[ \left( \frac{dy}{dx} \right)^{- 1} \right] \cdot \frac{dx}{dy} = - \left( \frac{dy}{dx} \right)^{- 2} \cdot \frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}} \cdot \left( \frac{dy}{dx} \right)^{- 1} = - \left( \frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}} \right)\left( \frac{dy}{dx} \right)^{- 3}.\]
IIT200700002Q49:
Separate the variables in \(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{\sqrt{1 - y^{2}}}{y}\):
\[\frac{y\ dy}{\sqrt{1 - y^{2}}} = dx.\]
Integrating both sides gives \(- \sqrt{1 - y^{2}} = x - C\). Squaring both sides:
\[(x - C)^{2} + y^{2} = 1,\]
which represents a family of circles with fixed radius \(1\) and variable centres \((C, 0)\) along the \(x\)-axis.
IIT200700002Q50:
Given \(\overrightarrow{a} + \overrightarrow{b} + \overrightarrow{c} = \overrightarrow{0}\), taking the cross product with \(\overrightarrow{a}\) on the left gives:
\[\overrightarrow{a} \times \left( \overrightarrow{a} + \overrightarrow{b} + \overrightarrow{c} \right) = \overrightarrow{0} \Longrightarrow \overrightarrow{0} + \overrightarrow{a} \times \overrightarrow{b} + \overrightarrow{a} \times \overrightarrow{c} = \overrightarrow{0} \Longrightarrow \overrightarrow{a} \times \overrightarrow{b} = \overrightarrow{c} \times \overrightarrow{a}.\]
Similarly, taking the cross product with \(\overrightarrow{b}\) gives \(\overrightarrow{a} \times \overrightarrow{b} = \overrightarrow{b} \times \overrightarrow{c}\).
Since \(\left| \overrightarrow{a} \right| = \left| \overrightarrow{b} \right| = \left| \overrightarrow{c} \right| = 1\) and \(\overrightarrow{a} + \overrightarrow{b} + \overrightarrow{c} = \overrightarrow{0}\), the three vectors form an equilateral triangle (angles of \(120^{{^\circ}}\) between any two), so \(\left| \overrightarrow{a} \times \overrightarrow{b} \right| = sin\ 120^{{^\circ}} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \neq 0\).
Hence, \(\overrightarrow{a} \times \overrightarrow{b} = \overrightarrow{b} \times \overrightarrow{c} = \overrightarrow{c} \times \overrightarrow{a} \neq \overrightarrow{0}\).
IIT200700002Q51:
Let \(r\) be the radius of the inscribed circle. Since \(AB \parallel CD\) and \(AD\bot AB\), the height of the right trapezium \(ABCD\) is \(AD = 2r\).
Let \(CD = a\), so \(AB = 2a\). Dropping a perpendicular from \(C\) to \(AB\) shows that the slanted side has length \(BC = \sqrt{AD^{2} + (AB - CD)^{2}} = \sqrt{4r^{2} + a^{2}}\).
Since a circle is inscribed in quadrilateral \(ABCD\), the sums of opposite sides are equal (Pitot's theorem):
\[AB + CD = AD + BC \Longrightarrow 3a = 2r + \sqrt{4r^{2} + a^{2}} \Longrightarrow (3a - 2r)^{2} = 4r^{2} + a^{2} \Longrightarrow 8a^{2} = 12ar \Longrightarrow a = \frac{3}{2}r.\]
The area of trapezium \(ABCD\) is \(\frac{1}{2}(AB + CD) \cdot AD = \frac{1}{2}(3a)(2r) = 3ar = 3\left( \frac{3}{2}r \right)r = \frac{9}{2}r^{2} = 18 \Longrightarrow r^{2} = 4 \Longrightarrow r = 2\).
IIT200700002Q52:
Given \(f(x) = \frac{x}{\left( 1 + x^{n} \right)^{1/n}}\), compute successive compositions:
\[(f \circ f)(x) = \frac{f(x)}{\left( 1 + \left( f(x) \right)^{n} \right)^{1/n}} = \frac{\frac{x}{\left( 1 + x^{n} \right)^{1/n}}}{\left( 1 + \frac{x^{n}}{1 + x^{n}} \right)^{1/n}} = \frac{x}{\left( 1 + 2x^{n} \right)^{1/n}}.\]
By induction on the number of compositions \(k\), the \(n\)-fold composition is \(g(x) = \frac{x}{\left( 1 + nx^{n} \right)^{1/n}}\).
Substituting \(g(x)\) into the integral gives \(I = \int x^{n - 2}g(x)\ dx = \int\frac{x^{n - 1}}{\left( 1 + nx^{n} \right)^{1/n}}\ dx\).
Let \(u = 1 + nx^{n}\), so \(du = n^{2}x^{n - 1}\ dx \Longrightarrow x^{n - 1}\ dx = \frac{du}{n^{2}}\):
\[I = \frac{1}{n^{2}}\int u^{- 1/n}\ du = \frac{1}{n^{2}} \cdot \frac{u^{1 - 1/n}}{1 - \frac{1}{n}} + K = \frac{1}{n(n - 1)}\left( 1 + nx^{n} \right)^{1 - \frac{1}{n}} + K.\]
IIT200700002Q53:
The \(6\) letters of COCHIN in alphabetical order are \(\text{C}, \text{C}, \text{H}, \text{I}, \text{N}, \text{O}\).
In dictionary order, any word starting with \(\text{C}\) followed by a second letter alphabetically smaller than \(\text{O}\) comes before COCHIN:
